# Terminal Launch Feature ## Overview Commands can now execute in **visible terminal windows** instead of hidden background processes. This solves multiple critical UX and functionality issues: - ✅ **Interactive Commands**: Password prompts (`sudo`), editors (`vim`), monitors (`top`) now work - ✅ **Transparency**: See exactly what's executing in real-time - ✅ **Security**: Passwords typed in real terminal, not web UI - ✅ **Debugging**: Direct terminal access for troubleshooting - ✅ **User Control**: Choose execution mode per command - ✅ **Cancellation**: Commands can be aborted with proper cleanup - ✅ **Error Handling**: Partial output preserved when commands fail or are cancelled ## How It Works ### Execution Modes **🖥️ Terminal Mode**: - Opens OS native terminal window - Command runs visibly with full terminal features - Interactive prompts work (passwords, confirmations) - Terminal stays open after completion - Best for: `sudo`, `ssh`, `vim`, `top`, `tail -f` **⚡ Background Mode**: - Runs invisibly, captures output - Results shown in chat - No stdin/interaction possible - Fast for simple commands - Best for: `ls`, `pwd`, `git status`, `cat file.txt` ### Smart Defaults The system **automatically suggests** the best execution mode based on command pattern detection. **Auto-selects Terminal for Interactive Commands**: - `sudo` - password input needed - `su ` - switch user (password required) - `ssh` - remote shell/may need credentials - `scp` - secure copy (may need password) - `vim`, `vi `, `nano`, `emacs` - text editors - `less`, `more` - pagers - `top`, `htop` - process monitors - `watch` - continuous monitoring - `tail -f` - log following - `docker exec -it`, `kubectl exec -it` - interactive containers - `python -i`, `node ` - REPLs - `irb` - Ruby REPL - `psql` - PostgreSQL shell - `mysql` - MySQL shell - `redis-cli` - Redis CLI **Auto-selects Background for Non-Interactive Commands**: - `ls`, `pwd`, `cd` - directory operations - `cat`, `head`, `tail` (without -f) - file viewing - `git status`, `git log` - git queries - `echo`, `printf` - output commands - Most build/compilation commands - Simple script execution ### User Override Users can always override the suggestion: - Modal shows both options - Recommendation highlighted when applicable - Choice remembered for session (optional) ## Command Lifecycle & Cancellation ### Command Execution States 1. **Pending**: User approval required (modal shown) 2. **Running**: Command executing (background or terminal) 3. **Completed**: Finished with exit code 4. **Cancelled**: User-initiated abort 5. **Failed**: Error during execution ### Cancellation Support (Background Mode) **User-Initiated Cancellation**: - Frontend sends abort signal via `AbortController` - Backend detects context cancellation - Process killed via `syscall.Kill(-pid, SIGKILL)` - Process group ensures child processes also terminated - Partial output captured before cancellation - Response marked with `cancelled: true` **Implementation Details**: ```go // Process group support for Unix cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{ Setpgid: true, // Create new process group } // Kill entire process tree on cancellation syscall.Kill(-cmd.Process.Pid, syscall.SIGKILL) ``` **Cancellation Response**: ```json { "cancelled": true, "exit_code": -1, "stdout": "partial output before cancellation", "stderr": "partial errors if any", "error": "context cancelled: command aborted by user" } ``` **UI Display**: ``` ⚠️ Command Cancelled ⚡ Background Command: `sleep 10 && echo done` Status: The command was stopped by user request. Partial Output (before cancellation): ``` [Any output captured before abort] ``` ``` ### Error Handling with Partial Output **Graceful Failure Handling**: - Commands that fail naturally (exit code != 0) preserve all output - Stdout and stderr captured even when command errors - Error message includes exit code and reason - UI distinguishes between cancelled vs failed states **Failed Command Response**: ```json { "cancelled": false, "exit_code": 1, "stdout": "output before failure", "stderr": "error messages", "error": "exit status 1" } ``` **Terminal Mode Cancellation**: - User presses Ctrl+C directly in terminal window - Terminal handles process interruption - No special backend logic needed - Natural terminal behavior preserved ## Implementation ### Backend (Daemon) **New File**: `lib/sop/cmd/sop-daemon/terminal.go` Cross-platform terminal launcher: ```go func launchInTerminal(command, workingDir string) error ``` Platform-specific implementations: - **macOS**: Uses AppleScript → Terminal.app - **Linux**: Tries gnome-terminal, konsole, xterm, etc. - **Windows**: Uses Windows Terminal or cmd.exe **Detection Functions**: ```go func shouldUseTerminal(command string) bool func getTerminalSuggestion(command string) string ``` **Updated**: `lib/sop/cmd/sop-daemon/main.go` ExecuteRequest now includes: ```go type ExecuteRequest struct { Command string `json:"command"` WorkingDir string `json:"working_dir,omitempty"` ExecutionMode string `json:"execution_mode,omitempty"` // "terminal" or "background" // ... other fields } ``` ExecuteResponse includes: ```go type ExecuteResponse struct { Stdout string `json:"stdout"` Stderr string `json:"stderr"` ExitCode int `json:"exit_code"` Error string `json:"error,omitempty"` Cancelled bool `json:"cancelled,omitempty"` // NEW: User-initiated abort LaunchedInTerminal bool `json:"launched_in_terminal,omitempty"` Suggestion string `json:"suggestion,omitempty"` // ... other fields } ``` **Execution Flow**: 1. Parse `execution_mode` from request ("terminal" or "background") 2. Auto-detect if not specified using `shouldUseTerminal()` 3. Terminal mode: Launch via `launchInTerminal()` and return immediately 4. Background mode: Execute with context cancellation support 5. Monitor for context.Done() signal during execution 6. On cancellation: Kill process group and capture partial output 7. On completion: Return full output with exit code **Terminal Launch Messages**: When commands launch in terminal, the chat window displays: ``` ✅ Command Launched in Terminal Window 🖥️ Command: `sudo apt update` What's happening: • A terminal window has opened on your system • The command is running there with full terminal capabilities • You can interact with it directly (passwords, prompts, etc.) After the command completes: • Return to this chat window to continue • The terminal will prompt "Press any key to close..." • You can then tell me about the results or ask follow-up questions ``` ### Frontend (Web UI) **Updated**: `lib/sop/tools/sopbackend/templates/modals.html` Approval modal now includes execution mode selection: ```html
🖥️ Launch in Terminal Window ⚡ Run in Background
💡 Suggestion: [context-specific tip]
``` **Updated**: `lib/sop/tools/sopbackend/templates/scripts_part05.html` JavaScript functions: ```javascript shouldUseTerminal(command) // Detects interactive commands getTerminalSuggestion(command) // Explains why terminal is suggested showActionApprovalModal(payload) // Sets smart defaults executeApprovedAction(...) // Handles execution mode ``` ## Usage Examples ### Example 1: sudo Command (Auto-Terminal) ``` User: "Run sudo apt update" [Approval Modal Appears] ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ⚠️ Action Requires Approval │ │ │ │ Command: sudo apt update │ │ │ │ Execution Mode: │ │ ● 🖥️ Launch in Terminal Window │ │ Opens a visible terminal │ │ │ │ ○ ⚡ Run in Background │ │ Captures output to chat │ │ │ │ 💡 This command requires password │ │ input - terminal window │ │ recommended │ │ │ │ [Deny] [Allow] │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ User clicks [Allow] ✅ Command Launched in Terminal 🖥️ Command: sudo apt update The command is running in a visible terminal window. Check your system for the terminal window to see output and provide input if needed. [macOS: Terminal.app window opens] [User types password in terminal] [Sees apt update progress] [Terminal shows: Press any key to close...] ``` ### Example 2: Simple Command (Auto-Background) ``` User: "Show me the current directory" [Approval Modal Appears] ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ⚠️ Action Requires Approval │ │ │ │ Command: pwd │ │ │ │ Execution Mode: │ │ ○ 🖥️ Launch in Terminal Window │ │ │ │ ● ⚡ Run in Background (default) │ │ Fast for simple commands │ │ │ │ [Deny] [Allow] │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ User clicks [Allow] ✅ Local Command Executed ⚡ Background Command: pwd Output: ``` /Users/user/project ``` Exit Code: 0 ``` ### Example 3: Override Suggestion ``` User: "Run tail -f app.log" [Approval Modal Appears] Modal suggests: 🖥️ Terminal (for real-time viewing) User thinks: "I just want to see a few lines" User selects: ⚡ Background User clicks [Allow] ✅ Local Command Executed ⚡ Background Command: tail -f app.log [Shows last 10 lines in chat] 💡 Tip: Log following is easier to view in terminal window. Consider using terminal mode for continuous monitoring. ``` ## Platform-Specific Behavior ### macOS **Terminal**: Terminal.app (via AppleScript) ```applescript tell application "Terminal" activate do script "cd '/path' && command; echo ''; echo 'Press any key to close...'; read -n 1" end tell ``` **Features**: - ✅ Opens new Terminal.app tab/window - ✅ Changes to working directory - ✅ Runs command - ✅ Waits for keypress before closing - ✅ Terminal.app icon bounces in Dock ### Linux **Terminal**: Tries in order: gnome-terminal, konsole, xfce4-terminal, xterm, x-terminal-emulator ```bash gnome-terminal -- bash -c "cd '/path' && command; echo ''; echo 'Press any key to close...'; read -n 1" ``` **Features**: - ✅ Opens default terminal emulator - ✅ Works with most desktop environments (GNOME, KDE, XFCE) - ✅ Fallback chain for compatibility - ✅ Terminal stays visible after completion ### Windows **Terminal**: Windows Terminal (wt.exe) or cmd.exe ```cmd wt.exe new-tab cmd /k "cd /d C:\path && command && echo. && echo Press any key to close... && pause > nul" ``` **Features**: - ✅ Prefers modern Windows Terminal if available - ✅ Falls back to classic cmd.exe - ✅ Changes directory correctly - ✅ Pauses before closing ## Session Approval Integration Works seamlessly with session auto-approval: ``` User enables "Always allow shell commands for this session" User selects "Terminal mode" Next 10 commands automatically launch in terminal: - sudo apt install package → Terminal opens - sudo systemctl restart app → Terminal opens - ssh user@server → Terminal opens [All without approval prompts] ``` ## Error Handling ### Terminal Launch Fails If terminal can't launch (no terminal emulator found, permission issue): ``` 1. Log error: "Failed to launch terminal: [error]" 2. Automatically fall back to background mode 3. Attempt execution in background 4. Show warning in chat if background also fails ``` ### Background Execution Issues If command needs interaction but runs in background: ``` Command executes but: - Stdin not connected (prompts fail) - Exit code indicates error - Response includes suggestion 💡 Tip: This command requires password input - terminal window recommended ``` ## Security Considerations ### Passwords in Terminal ✅ **Secure Approach**: - Password prompt appears in **OS terminal** - User types password using **system keychain integration** - Password **never** touches web stack - No JavaScript, no browser, no network **Why This Is Safe**: - Terminal is OS-controlled, not web-controlled - Same security as running commands manually - Follows industry best practices (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) - Zero additional attack surface ### Command Visibility 👁️ **Transparency**: - User **sees** terminal open (knows something is running) - Can **read** entire command before execution - Can **interrupt** with Ctrl+C if needed - Can **inspect** output in real-time ### Audit Trail Daemon logs every execution: ``` [Daemon Log] 2026-07-07 14:23:15 Executing command in terminal mode: sudo apt update 2026-07-07 14:23:16 Command launched in terminal successfully ``` ## Configuration ### User Preferences (Future Enhancement) ```javascript // localStorage: terminal_preferences { "default_mode": "auto", // auto, terminal, background "always_terminal": ["sudo", "ssh"], "always_background": ["ls", "pwd"], "remember_choice": true } ``` ### Daemon Configuration No configuration needed - works out of the box. Optional environment variables: ```bash # Override default terminal (Linux) export SOP_TERMINAL=konsole # Disable terminal launch (force background) export SOP_DISABLE_TERMINAL=true ``` ## Troubleshooting ### Terminal Doesn't Open **Symptoms**: Approval granted, but no terminal appears **Checks**: 1. Check daemon logs: `tail -f /path/to/daemon.log` 2. Look for: "Failed to launch terminal: [error]" 3. Verify terminal emulator installed: - macOS: Terminal.app exists (built-in) - Linux: `which gnome-terminal` or `which xterm` - Windows: `where wt.exe` or `where cmd.exe` **Solutions**: - Install a terminal emulator - Use background mode instead - Check terminal emulator permissions ### Command Hangs in Background **Symptoms**: Background execution times out, no output **Reason**: Command needs interaction but stdin not connected **Solution**: Use terminal mode for: - Commands with `sudo` - SSH connections - Text editors - Any prompt-based command ### Terminal Closes Immediately **Expected Behavior**: Terminal shows "Press any key to close..." **If not working**: - macOS: AppleScript adds pause automatically - Linux: Check terminal emulator support for `-e` flag - Windows: `pause` command should work ## Testing ### Manual Test Cases #### Test 1: sudo Command ```bash Command: sudo echo "test" Expected: Terminal opens, prompts for password, shows output, waits for key ``` #### Test 2: Simple Command ```bash Command: ls -la Expected: Background execution, output in chat ``` #### Test 3: Interactive Editor ```bash Command: vim test.txt Expected: Terminal opens, vim works fully, editable ``` #### Test 4: Log Following ```bash Command: tail -f /var/log/syslog Expected: Terminal opens, shows real-time log updates ``` #### Test 5: Fallback ```bash Scenario: Terminal launch fails Expected: Falls back to background, shows warning ``` #### Test 6: Command Cancellation ```bash Command: sleep 10 && echo done Action: Click cancel button during execution Expected: Command aborted within 0.10s, partial output shown ``` #### Test 7: Partial Output on Error ```bash Command: echo 'partial output' && exit 1 Expected: Shows "partial output" even though command failed, exit code 1 ``` ### Automated Tests **Run all daemon tests**: ```bash cd /Volumes/T7/sop-cloud/lib/sop go test ./cmd/sop-daemon/ -v ``` **Key test functions**: - `TestExecuteHandlerRunsShellCommand` - Basic command execution - `TestExecuteHandlerHandlesCancellation` - Context cancellation (0.10s completion) - `TestExecuteHandlerShowsPartialOutputOnError` - Partial output preservation - `TestShouldUseTerminal` - Pattern detection logic - `TestGetTerminalSuggestion` - Suggestion text generation **Test coverage**: - 97+ tests covering command execution - Process group termination - Cancellation flow (verify fast termination) - Error handling with output preservation - Terminal detection patterns ## Future Enhancements ### Phase 2: Bidirectional Communication Stream terminal output back to web UI while keeping it visible: - WebSocket connection to terminal - Real-time output in both terminal and chat - Best of both worlds ### Phase 3: Terminal Sessions Persist terminal sessions: - Reconnect to existing terminal - Multiple commands in same session - Session history and replay ### Phase 4: Custom Terminal Profiles User-defined terminal configurations: - Color schemes - Font sizes - Working directory preferences - Environment variables ## Comparison with Industry ### VS Code - ✅ Shows terminal panel for tasks - ✅ Interactive input works - ✅ User sees what's executing - **Similar to our terminal mode** ### GitHub Desktop - ✅ Terminal panel for git operations - ✅ Visual feedback on commands - **Similar to our terminal mode** ### Docker Desktop - ✅ Terminal for container exec - ✅ Interactive shells work - **Similar to our terminal mode** ### Our Implementation - ✅ **Better**: Uses native terminal (more familiar) - ✅ **Better**: Works with any command (not just predefined) - ✅ **Better**: User choice (terminal or background) - ✅ **Better**: Smart defaults (auto-detect interactive) ## Summary The terminal launch feature transforms the approval system from **passive** (show output after) to **active** (show execution live): **Before**: - Commands run invisibly - Interactive commands fail - No password input possible - Hard to debug - User doesn't see what's happening **After**: - Commands run visibly (if chosen) - Interactive commands work ✅ - Passwords typed in secure terminal ✅ - Easy to debug ✅ - Full transparency ✅ - User maintains control ✅ This is a **production-ready** implementation following industry best practices for desktop automation tools. --- ## Decision Flow Diagram ``` ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ User Request (Command) │ └──────────┬──────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Approval Modal Appears │ │ - Shows command │ │ - Shows execution mode │ │ - Smart default selected │ └──────────┬──────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────┐ │ Mode Check │ │ execution_ │ │ mode set? │ └──┬───────┬───┘ │ │ NO YES │ │ ▼ │ ┌──────────┐ │ │shouldUse │ │ │Terminal()│ │ └──┬───┬───┘ │ │ │ │ YES NO │ │ │ │ │ └─────┤ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │Terminal│ │Background│ │ Mode │ │ Mode │ └───┬────┘ └────┬─────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │Launch │ │Execute with │ │Terminal│ │Context Monitoring│ │Window │ └────┬─────────────┘ └────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Running... │ │ │ │ Wait for: │ │ - # Platform Foundations

This category captures the core architectural model, platform abstractions, and design assumptions that define how SOP works.

## Architecture

This category explains the backend topology, registry-centered consistency model, and storage layouts that underpin SOP deployments.

- Item: Filesystem and hybrid backend model
  Summary: SOP supports a filesystem backend and a hybrid Cassandra-backed metadata backend.
  Summary: The filesystem backend stores registry metadata in a filesystem-native mapped structure.
  Summary: The hybrid backend stores registry metadata in Cassandra while keeping blobs on the filesystem.
  Summary: Both backends share the same transactional model and differ mainly in registry placement and operational tradeoffs.
  Body:
  SOP exposes two primary backend models. The recommended `infs` backend stores both metadata and data on the filesystem, using Redis only for distributed locking and caching. The `incfs` backend stores registry metadata in Cassandra while keeping B-Tree nodes and data values in the filesystem blob store. In both cases, the transaction model is the same: writes prepare data first and then make them durable by updating the registry layer.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md, README.md

- Item: Registry as source of truth
  Summary: SOP uses the registry as the authoritative mapping from logical IDs to physical locations.
  Summary: Registry updates define the commit point for copy-on-write object replacement.
  Summary: Local cache staleness is avoided by looking up current physical handles through the registry first.
  Body:
  SOP identifies nodes and items through logical IDs and uses the registry to map them to current physical locations. This allows copy-on-write updates without breaking references. During reads, clients consult the registry before relying on local cache entries, which avoids returning stale values from older physical versions. During commit, the registry update is the durable transition from prepared artifacts to live state.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md

## Core Concepts

This category defines the main platform concepts that separate structured persistence, semantic memory, and shared runtime surfaces.

- Item: Stores and Spaces as separate domains
  Summary: SOP separates deterministic Stores from semantic Spaces.
  Summary: Stores are for structured B-Tree persistence and Spaces are for knowledge-oriented semantic memory.
  Summary: Both domains can coexist in the same product while serving different operational needs.
  Body:
  Stores are the general-purpose persistence surface for key-value data, structured records, joins, CRUD operations, and transaction-oriented workflows. Spaces are the semantic memory surface used for knowledge categories, items, vectorization, and retrieval. This distinction keeps structured persistence and semantic retrieval aligned without forcing them into one abstraction.
  Sources: README.md, WORKFLOWS.md, ai/README.md

- Item: System database role
  Summary: Every SOP environment includes a SystemDB for platform metadata and runtime artifacts.
  Summary: SystemDB stores scripts, knowledge, and other internal state used by the runtime.
  Summary: User databases and semantic spaces are separate from this shared system layer.
  Body:
  SOP provisions a built-in SystemDB in each environment. It stores internal metadata and runtime artifacts such as automation scripts, operational knowledge, and other system-level records. This keeps shared runtime state separate from application data stores and semantic spaces while preserving the same transactional model across the platform.
  Sources: README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md

## Design Principles

This category records the guiding design choices that shape SOP APIs, retrieval structure, and backend encapsulation.

- Item: Bounded semantic topology over raw heading structure
  Summary: The curated KB should use a stable semantic taxonomy instead of raw document headings.
  Summary: Category hierarchy should be bounded, reusable, and intentionally designed for retrieval.
  Summary: Headings define semantic topology while item summaries define vector indexing payload.
  Body:
  The curated knowledge source should not mirror arbitrary repository heading trees. Instead, it should define a bounded semantic hierarchy that is intentionally designed for retrieval. The heading structure determines the category graph, and the explicit item summaries under those headings provide the vector-facing indexing surface. This allows prompts to target meaningful categories and then match items through concise semantic summaries.
  Sources: ai/KB_CURATION_MANIFEST.md, ai/cmd/knowledge_compiler/README.md

- Item: Encapsulation and backend abstraction
  Summary: SOP keeps complex storage details behind high-level public packages.
  Summary: Internal packages hold lower-level backend logic that should not leak into consumer contracts.
  Summary: Public features are exposed through stable packages such as `infs`, `incfs`, and higher-level database APIs.
  Body:
  SOP separates public APIs from internal storage mechanics so consumers can rely on stable higher-level packages without coupling to low-level blob or registry details. This is especially important for the hybrid backend, where internal Cassandra/blob mechanics remain encapsulated while public packages expose transactional behavior through consistent APIs.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md

## Data Model & Abstractions

This category covers the abstractions that expose SOP data structures, schemas, and high-level database interfaces.

- Item: Metadata-carrying keys
  Summary: SOP supports complex B-Tree keys that carry state and routing metadata.
  Summary: Key fields can hold version, status, deletion, category, or vector-routing metadata.
  Summary: This allows many structural operations to run without loading the heavier value payload.
  Body:
  SOP does not treat keys as opaque strings only. Keys can be structured objects that carry state such as version, deleted flags, routing identifiers, or category information. This enables scans and filters to operate on key material directly, which reduces value fetches for common structural tasks and is used in both general data stores and vector-oriented paths.
  Sources: README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, ai/README.md

- Item: Unified database abstraction
  Summary: SOP provides a high-level database abstraction over stores, vectors, search, and models.
  Summary: Applications can use one entry point to open different persistence surfaces while sharing transactions.
  Summary: This abstraction supports both standalone and clustered deployments.
  Body:
  The database abstraction gives applications a single entry point for opening B-Trees, vector stores, search indexes, and model stores. It reduces configuration duplication and allows different persistence surfaces to participate in the same transactional flow where appropriate.
  Sources: README.md, GO_CORE_ENGINE.md, ai/README.md

- Item: Flat table abstraction over key-value storage
  Summary: SOP exposes stores to AI and application layers as flat table-like schemas rather than raw key and value wrappers.
  Summary: `key_fields` and `value_fields` identify structure without forcing nested Key or Value prefixes into queries.
  Summary: Relations and predicates operate on schema field names directly.
  Body:
  Internally, SOP stores data as structured key-value pairs in B-Trees, but the higher-level schema model removes those wrappers and presents a table abstraction. Fields appear at one flat level, primary-key components are identified explicitly, and relation mappings use schema field names directly. This keeps storage efficient while making query planning, joins, and AI-facing tooling easier to reason about.
  Sources: TABLE_ABSTRACTION.md, README.md

# Installation & Setup

This category covers the environment requirements, configuration model, and setup flows needed to run SOP.

## Prerequisites

This category summarizes the runtime dependencies and platform requirements needed before installing or deploying SOP.

- Item: Core runtime prerequisites
  Summary: Go is the primary prerequisite for native SOP development.
  Summary: Redis is optional for standalone use and required for clustered coordination.
  Summary: Cassandra is only required when the hybrid backend is selected.
  Body:
  Native development with SOP requires Go. Redis is not required for standalone deployments using in-memory coordination, but clustered deployments depend on Redis for lock coordination and caching. Cassandra is only needed when the `incfs` backend is used for metadata storage.
  Sources: GETTING_STARTED.md, OPERATIONS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md

## Configuration

This category describes the configuration knobs that control storage layout, redundancy, caching, and performance behavior.

- Item: Storage redundancy configuration split
  Summary: SOP configures registry redundancy separately from user-data striping.
  Summary: `StoresFolders` controls registry and system-table redundancy.
  Summary: `ErasureConfigs` controls striping and parity for user data files.
  Body:
  SOP separates system-critical metadata configuration from bulk data configuration. `StoresFolders` define the registry and system-table partitions, usually with active/passive failover. `ErasureConfigs` define how user data is striped and protected through Reed-Solomon parity. This split lets operators choose different durability and performance strategies for metadata and bulk content.
  Sources: CONFIGURATION.md, README.md

- Item: Cache and persistence tuning
  Summary: SOP exposes configuration for cache layers, blob placement, and node density.
  Summary: `SlotLength`, cache TTLs, and active persistence settings influence throughput and memory usage.
  Summary: Large-object workloads are expected to keep the B-Tree lean and push values into blobs.
  Body:
  Configuration and tuning revolve around balancing node density, cache reuse, and blob storage behavior. `SlotLength` influences B-Tree node density. Cache factory and store cache settings control TTL and backend selection. Large-object workloads typically use active persistence and blob storage so commits stay smaller and index structures remain efficient.
  Sources: CONFIGURATION.md

## Environment Setup

This category covers first-run provisioning, setup wizards, and language-specific installation paths for getting started.

- Item: Data Manager setup wizard
  Summary: The Data Manager setup wizard initializes deployment mode, storage paths, and optional demo data.
  Summary: Standalone mode uses local folders while clustered mode adds Redis-backed coordination.
  Summary: First-run setup creates the system database and an initial user database.
  Body:
  After launching the SOP HTTP Server, users interact with a web-based Setup Wizard to choose Standalone or Clustered mode, configure storage folders, optionally define erasure-coding settings, and preload demo data. The wizard provisions the SystemDB and one or more user databases so applications and the Data Manager can start operating immediately.
  Sources: docs/installation/DATA_MANAGER_SETUP.md, GETTING_STARTED.md

- Item: Language-specific installation paths
  Summary: Go integrates directly through modules, while other bindings use packaged artifacts or platform bundles.
  Summary: Python uses pip, C# uses NuGet, Java uses JAR-based distribution, and Rust uses Cargo and FFI bindings.
  Summary: Platform bundles include the Data Manager binary and language-specific assets for non-Go workflows.
  Body:
  SOP supports several installation paths depending on language. Go developers import the module directly. Python, C#, Java, and Rust developers consume packaged artifacts or platform bundles that include shared libraries and related tooling. This keeps the runtime consistent while matching the expected packaging model of each language ecosystem.
  Sources: docs/installation/LANGUAGE_BINDINGS.md, GETTING_STARTED.md, bindings/python/README.md, bindings/csharp/README.md, bindings/java/README.md, bindings/rust/README.md

## Deployment Modes

This category explains the supported deployment topologies and how standalone and clustered modes differ operationally.

- Item: Standalone and clustered deployment modes
  Summary: SOP supports standalone and clustered deployment modes.
  Summary: Standalone mode can use in-memory coordination without Redis.
  Summary: Clustered mode uses Redis-backed coordination and shared storage paths.
  Body:
  Standalone mode is intended for local, embedded, or single-process deployments and can use in-memory locking and caching. Clustered mode relies on Redis for coordination and usually pairs with shared or mounted storage. Both modes use the same storage and transaction concepts, but differ in coordination and deployment topology.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md, GETTING_STARTED.md, WORKFLOWS.md

# Storage & Data Management

This category describes how SOP stores, coordinates, and serves structured and semantic data across its persistence surfaces.

## Stores vs Spaces

This category distinguishes the structured store model from the semantic space model so each is used for the right workload.

- Item: Stores for structure, Spaces for semantics
  Summary: Stores are optimized for structured persistence and query workflows.
  Summary: Spaces are optimized for category-oriented semantic memory and retrieval.
  Summary: The split helps preserve strong transactional workflows without diluting semantic retrieval design.
  Body:
  Stores are the deterministic data-management path for B-Trees, structured records, joins, CRUD operations, and transactional logic. Spaces are the semantic path for knowledge categories, items, vectorization, and memory-oriented retrieval. Both remain first-class, but they serve different workloads and should not be treated as interchangeable abstractions.
  Sources: README.md, ai/README.md, WORKFLOWS.md, ai/agent/STORES_VS_SPACES.md

## Transactions

This category explains the commit model and consistency guarantees that let multiple SOP surfaces share one transactional foundation.

- Item: Commit-through-registry transaction model
  Summary: SOP uses a two-phase commit model built around prepared artifacts and registry updates.
  Summary: Prepared blobs become live only when registry handles are updated.
  Summary: This allows copy-on-write updates with ACID isolation across the storage model.
  Body:
  SOP writes modified nodes and values as prepared artifacts first. A transaction becomes durable only when the registry is updated to point at the new physical locations. This commit-through-registry model supports copy-on-write updates, rollback safety, and consistent reads without relying on a central database server process.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md

- Item: Multi-surface transactional consistency
  Summary: SOP can coordinate structured stores, search, and some AI-facing persistence under one transactional model.
  Summary: The system prefers one storage engine foundation across different data-management surfaces.
  Summary: This reduces divergence between operational data and AI-oriented persistence flows.
  Body:
  One of SOP's design goals is to keep different persistence features on a common transactional foundation. Structured stores, text search, model storage, and AI-facing layers all build on the same B-Tree and registry concepts. This allows operational and AI-related workloads to share consistency guarantees and minimizes the need for separate database products.
  Sources: README.md, ai/README.md, GO_CORE_ENGINE.md

## Caching & Consistency

This category covers how SOP balances cache performance with registry-based consistency and coordination.

- Item: Registry-first consistency model
  Summary: SOP uses registry lookups before trusting local caches.
  Summary: Redis is used for distributed locking and cache coordination rather than as the primary data store.
  Summary: The design avoids stale reads by resolving the current physical handle before value access.
  Body:
  SOP employs a multi-tier caching model, but consistency is anchored on the registry rather than blindly trusting local cache state. Clients resolve the current physical handle from the registry before using local data, which prevents stale reads after copy-on-write updates. Redis supplies distributed coordination and caching behavior, not the primary data persistence layer.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md, OPERATIONS.md

## Backend Options

This category compares the primary filesystem backend with the hybrid Cassandra-backed metadata option.

- Item: Filesystem backend as the primary deployment model
  Summary: The filesystem backend is the primary and recommended backend for most deployments.
  Summary: It stores data and registry structures on disk and uses Redis only for clustering concerns.
  Summary: It has outperformed the hybrid backend in the referenced repo stress tests.
  Body:
  The `infs` backend is the main storage model used across SOP. It keeps both registry and blob data on the filesystem and layers Redis coordination on top when clustering is required. This model keeps the operational stack smaller and, in the documented tests, performed better than the hybrid backend while retaining the same transactional behavior.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md, WORKFLOWS.md

- Item: Hybrid Cassandra backend for metadata replication
  Summary: The hybrid backend stores registry metadata in Cassandra while keeping blobs on the filesystem.
  Summary: It is appropriate when Cassandra infrastructure already exists or when metadata replication should follow Cassandra policies.
  Summary: Redis still supplies locking and caching for clustered coordination.
  Body:
  The `incfs` backend splits metadata and blob storage. Cassandra stores registry and root metadata, while B-Tree nodes and data blobs remain on the filesystem. This allows teams that already operate Cassandra clusters to reuse that infrastructure for metadata while keeping bulk data on disk and preserving SOP's transactional model.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md, WORKFLOWS.md, CONFIGURATION.md

## Filesystem / Redis / Cassandra

This category clarifies the distinct operational roles of filesystem storage, Redis coordination, and Cassandra metadata services.

- Item: Backend role separation
  Summary: Filesystem stores blobs and registry data in the main backend.
  Summary: Redis provides coordination and caching rather than primary persistence.
  Summary: Cassandra is only part of the hybrid backend and is used for registry metadata.
  Body:
  In the recommended backend, the filesystem stores both registry and blob data, while Redis handles coordination and cache distribution. In the hybrid backend, Cassandra replaces the filesystem registry layer for metadata, while blobs remain on disk. This separation keeps operational roles clear across the backend stack.
  Sources: ARCHITECTURE.md, CONFIGURATION.md, OPERATIONS.md

# Operations & Reliability

This category covers the testing, failure handling, tuning, observability, and security practices needed to operate SOP safely.

## Testing

This category summarizes how SOP validates behavior through unit, integration, stress, and reproducible Docker-based test flows.

- Item: Unit, integration, and stress test separation
  Summary: SOP test suites are separated into unit, integration, and stress scopes.
  Summary: Unit tests validate core behavior without external services.
  Summary: Integration and stress runs use explicit build tags and longer-running environments.
  Body:
  SOP uses default unit tests for fast local validation, while integration and stress scenarios are separated using build tags and specific task runners. This lets developers run lightweight validation during normal development and reserve Redis-, Cassandra-, or concurrency-heavy scenarios for integration environments and pre-release checks.
  Sources: README.md, WORKFLOWS.md, DEV_TOOLS.md

- Item: Docker-based reproducible test environments
  Summary: Docker-based test flows provide reproducible dependency and environment setup.
  Summary: Separate Docker files allow normal and no-coverage test runs.
  Summary: Root test scripts orchestrate broader multi-language or combined runs.
  Body:
  Docker-based testing helps keep environments reproducible across local and CI systems. The repository includes standard and no-coverage Docker flows along with shell scripts that orchestrate broader test suites. This reduces variation in dependency versions and runtime environment when validating the storage engine and related tooling.
  Sources: README.md, DEV_TOOLS.md

## Failover & Recovery

This category explains how SOP handles failover conditions, backup coordination, and recovery boundaries for durable storage.

- Item: Failover-qualified I/O errors
  Summary: SOP distinguishes transient errors from failover-qualified storage errors.
  Summary: Qualified errors include I/O failure, read-only filesystems, and no-space conditions.
  Summary: On qualified write failure, SOP switches to the configured standby path.
  Body:
  SOP does not treat every error as a failover event. Instead, it identifies specific storage failures such as `EIO`, `EROFS`, and `ENOSPC` as failover-qualified. When such an error occurs on a write path, the system marks the current storage path passive and continues on the configured active standby path. The failed path then requires intervention or repair.
  Sources: OPERATIONS.md

- Item: Backup and restore coordination
  Summary: Hybrid backup requires coordinated snapshots of Cassandra metadata and filesystem blobs.
  Summary: Consistent restore depends on restoring both registry state and blob content together.
  Summary: Copy-on-write behavior helps preserve point-in-time restore safety.
  Body:
  For the hybrid backend, operators snapshot Cassandra keyspace state and the blob filesystem together. If a zero-downtime snapshot is needed, the registry snapshot should be taken first and the filesystem snapshot second. Because SOP uses copy-on-write semantics, old blobs referenced by the older registry snapshot remain available long enough to preserve a consistent restore point.
  Sources: OPERATIONS.md

## Performance

This category describes the main throughput and scalability levers that affect SOP behavior in production.

- Item: Slot length as a density and throughput control
  Summary: `SlotLength` controls how many items live in a B-Tree node.
  Summary: Higher slot lengths increase density and can improve throughput for large datasets.
  Summary: Tradeoffs include node size, memory footprint, and workload-specific tuning.
  Body:
  `SlotLength` is one of the main B-Tree tuning levers in SOP. Larger values increase node density and reduce the number of traversed nodes, which can improve throughput for large datasets. The tradeoff is larger node size and potentially higher memory pressure. The configuration guide recommends tuning slot length by workload rather than treating one value as universal.
  Sources: CONFIGURATION.md, README.md, SCALABILITY.md

- Item: Scalability bounded by deployment design and hardware
  Summary: SOP scale is constrained primarily by storage, bandwidth, and coordination design.
  Summary: Registry partitioning and file layout are used to extend addressable capacity.
  Summary: Horizontal scaling depends on backend throughput, network capacity, and operational tuning.
  Body:
  SOP is designed so the practical scaling limit comes from hardware capacity and deployment architecture rather than from a central database server. Registry partitioning, segmented storage, and distributed coordination allow the system to address very large datasets, but actual throughput still depends on storage IOPS, network fabric, and how the cluster is tuned.

## Semantic Retrieval

This category describes the routing, distance math, and semantic anchor patterns that guide retrieval behavior.

- Item: Normalized-vector distance optimization
  Summary: SOP normalizes routing and category vectors once for the local Matryoshka path.
  Summary: For normalized vectors, Euclidean distance is computed from the dot product.
  Summary: The optimized formula is `sqrt(2 * (1 - dot(a, b)))` for unit vectors.
  Summary: This keeps Euclidean ordering while reducing repeated norm work in the search loop.
  Body:
  The memory math layer now uses a faster normalized-vector distance path for routing and category comparisons. Local Matryoshka-capable vectors are normalized at slice or index time, and distance calculations then use the dot-product-based Euclidean equivalent for unit vectors. This preserves the intended distance semantics while reducing hot-loop computation during search.

  Summary: This makes retrieval more targetable than raw document-level vector clouds.
  Body:
  The Dynamic Vector Store uses semantic anchors and category-level routing so the query first lands in the right conceptual neighborhood. Instead of relying only on mathematical clusters, the system maps content into semantically meaningful categories and then performs fine-grained matching within those domains. This makes retrieval easier to steer and easier to explain.

summaries: Functions should be synchronous by default; let callers add concurrency if they need it.

data.description: Prefer narrow interfaces that describe one capability well rather than large interfaces that bundle unrelated behavior. In Go, the interface surface should be as small as the use case requires. Many interfaces have just one or two methods. This keeps abstractions easier to understand and less brittle as code evolves. The smaller the interface, the more powerful the abstraction.
data.text: Keep interfaces small and focused
data.title: Keep interfaces small and focused

summaries: Broad interfaces weaken abstractions and make implementations harder to satisfy.

data.description: This makes APIs more flexible at the call site (accepting any implementation) while keeping return values concrete and discoverable. Don't force every type into an interface unnecessarily. Return interfaces only when you truly need polymorphism or expect the implementation to vary. Concrete return types are easier to document and use.
data.text: Accept interfaces, return concrete types
data.title: Accept interfaces, return concrete types

summaries: Function parameters should be interfaces when possible; return types should be concrete unless abstraction is needed.

data.description: Use a one- or two-character receiver name that reflects the type name (e.g., c c for Client Client, s s for Server Server). Be consistent: if one method uses c c, all methods on that type should use c c. Don't use this this or self self (those are not idiomatic Go). Avoid generic names like me me or t t unless they're truly unambiguous.
data.text: Use meaningful method receiver names
data.title: Use meaningful method receiver names

summaries: Method receiver names should be short but consistent across the type.

data.description: Use pointer receivers when the method modifies the receiver, when the receiver is large (copying would be expensive), or when consistency is needed (if some methods use pointers, all should). Use value receivers for small, immutable types. Be consistent within a type. Don't mix pointer and value receivers arbitrarily.
data.text: Choose pointer vs. value receivers intentionally
data.title: Choose pointer vs. value receivers intentionally

summaries: Method receivers should be pointers when they modify state or are large; otherwise use values.

data.description: Good package names are short, clear, and lowercase (e.g., http http, time time, fmt fmt). Avoid util util, common common, or generic names. The package name becomes part of the identifier (http.Get http.Get, time.Now time.Now), so it should add clarity. Don't stutter: if the package is log log, don't export LogWriter LogWriter; export Writer Writer and clients will see log.Writer log.Writer.
data.text: Use short, descriptive names for packages
data.title: Use short, descriptive names for packages

summaries: Package names should be lowercase, single-word, and evocative of purpose.

data.description: Multi-word names should be MixedCaps MixedCaps (exported) or mixedCaps mixedCaps (unexported). Never use underscores for separation (except in test files or when matching external naming). Initialisms should be consistent: use HTTP HTTP, URL URL, XML XML (all caps) or http http, url url, xml xml (all lowercase), not Http Http, Url Url, Xml Xml.
data.text: Use MixedCaps for multi-word names
data.title: Use MixedCaps for multi-word names

summaries: Go names use MixedCaps or mixedCaps, not underscores.

data.description: In a five-line function, i i is fine for a loop counter. In a 50-line function, use something more descriptive. The further from declaration a variable is used, the more descriptive its name should be. In tight scopes, clarity comes from compactness. In broad scopes, clarity comes from explicit naming.
data.text: Keep variable names short in small scopes
data.title: Keep variable names short in small scopes

summaries: Variable names should be shorter when their scope is smaller.

data.description: When code crosses package or service boundaries, pass context.Context context.Context as the first parameter (conventionally named ctx ctx) for deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped values. Avoid storing request state in globals or hidden mutable state. Don't store context in a struct; pass it explicitly. This keeps behavior predictable for long-running operations and network-bound work.
data.text: Use context for request-scoped values and cancellation
data.title: Use context for request-scoped values and cancellation

summaries: Context should carry deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped metadata through API boundaries.

data.description: This convention makes context usage consistent and easy to spot. Even if you don't use context now, adding it early makes future changes easier. Exception: methods on structs don't need to take context as a parameter if they're not performing operations that need cancellation (but if they later do, refactor to add it).
data.text: Context should be the first parameter
data.title: Context should be the first parameter

summaries: Functions accepting context should take it as the first parameter, named ctx ctx.

data.description: Never use context.Context as a way to avoid adding function parameters. Context is specifically for: (1) cancellation signals, (2) deadlines/timeouts, (3) request-scoped values like trace IDs, user identity, or request metadata. Do NOT use it for: business logic parameters, configuration values, dependencies, or application state. Misusing context makes function signatures unclear, breaks type safety, and makes code harder to test and understand. If you need to pass parameters, add them as explicit function arguments. If you have too many parameters, consider creating a struct. Context abuse is a common anti-pattern that violates Go idioms. Example of wrong usage: ctx.Value("userID") ctx.Value("userID") for a required parameter—this should be an explicit userID string userID string parameter instead.
data.text: Do not use context.Context to pass function parameters or state
data.title: Do not use context.Context to pass function parameters or state

summaries: Context is for deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped values only—not for passing normal function parameters.

data.description: Go testing often benefits from table-driven tests that describe a set of input and expected output cases. Define a slice of test cases with input and expected output, then loop over them. Keep test names clear, keep assertions direct, and avoid over-mocking. Tests should communicate the intended behavior of the code and protect against regressions. Name your test cases for easy debugging.
data.text: Write table-driven tests for behavior
data.title: Write table-driven tests for behavior

summaries: Tests should be readable, focused, and easy to extend.

data.description: Use t.Errorf("Foo(%q) = %d; want %d", input, got, want) t.Errorf("Foo(%q) = %d; want %d", input, got, want) rather than generic assertions. Always include the input that failed, the actual result, and the expected result. This makes debugging much faster. Avoid test helpers that obscure the failure message. The person debugging your test should understand the failure without reading the test code.
data.text: Write useful test failures with context
data.title: Write useful test failures with context

summaries: Test failures should say what was wrong, what input caused it, and what was expected.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Go/Common Gotchas and Anti-Patterns
data.description: var s []T var s []T declares a nil slice, while s := []T{} s := []T{} creates a non-nil but empty slice. They are functionally equivalent (len len and cap cap both 0), but nil is the preferred style because it's simpler and uses less memory. Exception: JSON encoding differs (nil nil becomes null null, []T{} []T{} becomes [] []), so use non-nil empty slices when that matters.
data.text: Declare empty slices as var s []T var s []T, not s := []T{} s := []T{}
data.title: Declare empty slices as var s []T var s []T, not s := []T{} s := []T{}

summaries: Prefer nil slices over non-nil empty slices.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Go/Common Gotchas and Anti-Patterns
data.description: Functions should return (T, error) (T, error) rather than returning a special value (like -1 or "") to indicate error. This makes the error explicit and allows callers to handle it properly. In-band errors are confusing, harder to check, and violate Go's explicit error handling philosophy.
data.text: Avoid in-band error values (like -1, "", etc.)
data.title: Avoid in-band error values (like -1, "", etc.)

summaries: Return explicit error values rather than special sentinel values.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Go/Common Gotchas and Anti-Patterns
data.description: Don't use . . imports (import . "fmt" import . "fmt") because they pollute the namespace and make it unclear where identifiers come from. Always use explicit package identifiers (fmt.Println fmt.Println). Exception: Test files can use dot imports for testing packages, but this should be rare.
data.text: Never use wildcard imports or dot imports
data.title: Never use wildcard imports or dot imports

summaries: Import packages explicitly with their full package name.

data.description: Doc comments should be complete sentences that start with the name being documented. For example: // Get fetches the value for a given key. // Get fetches the value for a given key. not // Fetches the value // Fetches the value or // This function gets... // This function gets.... Use periods. Doc comments appear in godoc, so make them clear and useful. If an API is complex, add examples in tests.
data.text: Write complete sentence doc comments starting with the name
data.title: Write complete sentence doc comments starting with the name

summaries: Every exported name should have a doc comment that starts with the name itself.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Java/File Organization and Structure
data.description: The standard Java convention is to place exactly one top-level public class, interface, or enum in each file, and the file name must match the class name. Private or package-private helper classes can exist in the same file but should be small. This improves navigation, keeps files predictable, and matches the expectations of most Java tools and code review workflows. Avoid creating "utility" files with multiple unrelated classes.
data.text: Keep one top-level type per file
data.title: Keep one top-level type per file

summaries: Java files should be organized around one primary public type to keep structure obvious.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Java/File Organization and Structure
data.description: Arrange class members in a consistent order: static fields, instance fields, constructors, methods. Group overloaded methods together. Arrange methods logically (e.g., public API first, then private helpers), not chronologically. This makes classes easier to navigate. Google style recommends grouping by functionality when it improves understanding.
data.text: Order class members consistently
data.title: Order class members consistently

summaries: Class members should follow a standard, predictable order.

data.description: Java code should use UpperCamelCase UpperCamelCase for class names and type parameters, camelCase camelCase for method names and variables, and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants (static final fields). Package names should be all lowercase without underscores (e.g., com.example.myproject com.example.myproject). Names should communicate purpose rather than implementation detail. Avoid abbreviations except for very common ones (id, url). Methods that return a boolean should start with is is, has has, or can can.
data.text: Use clear naming and package structure
data.title: Use clear naming and package structure

summaries: Types, methods, and packages should reflect intent and responsibility.

data.description: Avoid names like list list, map map, i i, or temp temp except in the narrowest scopes (single-letter names are acceptable for loop indices in short loops). Use names that describe what the variable represents: customers customers, orderById orderById, activeUserCount activeUserCount. The name should make the code self-documenting. For collections, prefer plural nouns.
data.text: Use intention-revealing names for variables
data.title: Use intention-revealing names for variables

summaries: Variable names should explain their purpose, not just their type.

data.description: Use K&R style: opening brace at the end of the line, closing brace on its own line, aligned with the beginning of the statement. Always use braces even for single-statement if/for/while blocks (this prevents bugs when code changes). Example: if (condition) { if (condition) { not if (condition)\n{ if (condition)\n{. This is the standard Java convention.
data.text: Use consistent brace style (K&R)
data.title: Use consistent brace style (K&R)

summaries: Opening braces go on the same line as the declaration; closing braces on their own line.

data.description: Google style recommends a column limit of 100 characters (some teams use 120). Exceptions: package statements, import statements, comments with long URLs. When wrapping, indent continuation lines at least +4 from the original line. Break at higher syntactic levels (e.g., before a dot in a chain of method calls).
data.text: Limit line length to 100 characters
data.title: Limit line length to 100 characters

summaries: Lines should wrap at a reasonable column to improve readability.

data.description: Never use wildcard imports (import java.util.*; import java.util.*;) because they reduce clarity and make dependencies harder to reason about. Import each class explicitly. Order imports in groups: static imports, then non-static imports in alphabetical order. Remove unused imports. This makes review and maintenance easier and avoids accidental namespace coupling. Most IDEs can auto-organize imports.
data.text: Avoid wildcard imports and keep imports explicit
data.title: Avoid wildcard imports and keep imports explicit

summaries: Imports should be clear and stable.

data.description: Avoid pulling in large dependencies for small utility functions. Make dependencies explicit through imports and constructor parameters rather than hiding them in static state. This makes testing easier and coupling more visible. Consider whether you really need that framework, or if a simpler approach would suffice.
data.text: Keep dependencies minimal and explicit
data.title: Keep dependencies minimal and explicit

summaries: Classes should depend only on what they actually use.

data.description: Always use @Override @Override when overriding a method from a superclass or implementing an interface method (Java 6+). This improves readability, helps catch mistakes when signatures change, and makes refactoring safer. If you remove a parent method and forget to update the child, the compiler will catch it. This is one of the most important Java annotations.
data.text: Use @Override @Override consistently
data.title: Use @Override @Override consistently

summaries: Override annotations should be present whenever a method overrides a parent method or implements an interface method.

data.description: Use @Deprecated @Deprecated when replacing old APIs, and include a Javadoc comment explaining what to use instead. Use @SuppressWarnings @SuppressWarnings sparingly and only for specific warnings with a comment explaining why it's safe. Use @Nullable @Nullable and @NonNull @NonNull (or similar annotations) to document nullability contracts. Don't overuse annotations; every annotation should serve a clear purpose.
data.text: Use standard annotations meaningfully
data.title: Use standard annotations meaningfully

summaries: Annotations like @Deprecated @Deprecated, @SuppressWarnings @SuppressWarnings, and @Nullable @Nullable should be used when they add value.

data.description: Catch specific exception types, not broad Exception Exception or Throwable Throwable. Avoid empty catch blocks (if you must ignore an exception, name the variable ignored ignored and add a comment). Never catch Throwable Throwable or Error Error. Use try-with-resources for any AutoCloseable AutoCloseable resource (files, streams, database connections). Preserve exception context: don't swallow exceptions or throw new ones without chaining. This makes code more robust and easier to debug.
data.text: Prefer specific exception handling and structured cleanup
data.title: Prefer specific exception handling and structured cleanup

summaries: Java code should handle real failure modes explicitly and close resources deterministically.

data.description: Don't use try-catch as a substitute for proper if-checks or validation. Exceptions are expensive and should represent actual error conditions. For example, checking if a value is present should use an Optional Optional or null check, not catching NoSuchElementException NoSuchElementException. This improves performance and makes the code intent clearer.
data.text: Don't use exceptions for control flow
data.title: Don't use exceptions for control flow

summaries: Exceptions should represent exceptional conditions, not normal program flow.

data.description: Modern Java (14+) provides powerful features: use records for simple data carriers, sealed classes for controlled inheritance, switch expressions for exhaustive matching, text blocks for multi-line strings, and pattern matching to reduce casting. These features reduce boilerplate and express intent more clearly. Don't force them where simpler constructs are clearer, but embrace them when they improve the code. Records are especially useful for DTOs, value objects, and immutable data.
data.text: Use modern Java features when they improve clarity
data.title: Use modern Java features when they improve clarity

summaries: Records, sealed types, switch expressions, text blocks, and pattern matching make code more expressive.

data.description: Use var var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side (var list = new ArrayList<String>() var list = new ArrayList<String>()). Avoid it when the type is not clear (var result = someComplexMethod() var result = someComplexMethod()). Good use of var var reduces noise; bad use reduces clarity. When in doubt, use an explicit type. Never use var var for fields, method parameters, or return types (not allowed anyway).
data.text: Prefer var var for obvious types, explicit types otherwise
data.title: Prefer var var for obvious types, explicit types otherwise

summaries: Local variable type inference (var var) should improve readability, not obscure it.

data.description: Methods should do one thing well. If a method is longer than one screen or does multiple unrelated tasks, split it. Classes should have a single clear responsibility. Avoid "god objects" that do everything. Small, focused classes and methods are easier to test, reuse, and understand. If you struggle to name a class or method, it probably has too many responsibilities.
data.text: Keep methods and classes focused
data.title: Keep methods and classes focused

summaries: Java classes and methods should stay cohesive and avoid unrelated responsibilities.

data.description: Deep inheritance hierarchies are fragile and hard to understand. Prefer composition (using objects with specific capabilities) over inheritance (extending classes). Use interfaces to define contracts. Inheritance is useful for clear "is-a" relationships, but composition is more flexible for "has-a" or "uses-a" relationships. Modern Java features like default interface methods make composition even more powerful.
data.text: Favor composition over inheritance
data.title: Favor composition over inheritance

summaries: Prefer building behavior from smaller pieces rather than complex inheritance hierarchies.

data.description: Declare method parameters using interface types (List List, Map Map, Set Set) rather than concrete implementations (ArrayList ArrayList, HashMap HashMap, HashSet HashSet). This makes the code more flexible and testable. Return concrete types only when the caller needs implementation-specific methods. For example, accept List<String> List<String> but consider whether you could accept Collection<String> Collection<String> or even Iterable<String> Iterable<String> to be even more flexible.
data.text: Program to interfaces, not implementations
data.title: Program to interfaces, not implementations

summaries: Method parameters and return types should be the most general interface that works.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Java/Immutability and Thread Safety
data.description: Prefer immutable classes (all fields final, no setters) when possible. Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe, easier to reason about, and prevent many bugs. Use builders for complex immutable objects. If you need mutability, document it clearly and consider whether the mutability should be encapsulated (private state with controlled mutation).
data.text: Make classes immutable by default
data.title: Make classes immutable by default

summaries: Immutable classes are simpler, safer, and more predictable.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Java/Immutability and Thread Safety
data.description: Every class that might be used concurrently should document its thread-safety guarantees in the class-level Javadoc: "This class is thread-safe" or "This class is not thread-safe and requires external synchronization." Don't leave it ambiguous. Use annotations like @ThreadSafe @ThreadSafe or @NotThreadSafe @NotThreadSafe if available. Synchronize only what needs synchronization; avoid over-synchronizing.
data.text: Document thread-safety guarantees
data.title: Document thread-safety guarantees

summaries: Classes should clearly document whether they are thread-safe.

data.description: Write complete, useful Javadoc for all public classes and methods. Describe what the class/method does, all parameters, return value, exceptions thrown, and any side effects. Use @param @param, @return @return, @throws @throws, and @deprecated @deprecated tags. Describe the contract, not the implementation. Bad Javadoc just repeats the method name; good Javadoc explains why the method exists and how to use it correctly. Include examples for complex APIs.
data.text: Document public APIs with Javadoc
data.title: Document public APIs with Javadoc

summaries: Every public class and public/protected method should have Javadoc.

data.description: Code should be self-explanatory through good naming. Use comments to explain why you made a choice, especially for non-obvious decisions. Avoid comments that just restate the code. Good comment: "Retry up to 3 times because the service is eventually consistent." Bad comment: "Set retries to 3." Document assumptions, invariants, and gotchas. Keep comments up to date; outdated comments are worse than no comments.
data.text: Write clear commit messages and code comments
data.title: Write clear commit messages and code comments

summaries: Comments should explain why, not what.

data.description: Use descriptive test names that explain what is being tested and what the expected outcome is (e.g., shouldReturnEmptyListWhenNoResults shouldReturnEmptyListWhenNoResults). Follow the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. One logical assertion per test. Tests should be independent and deterministic. Use mocks judiciously; prefer real objects when practical. Test behavior, not implementation details.
data.text: Write focused, readable unit tests
data.title: Write focused, readable unit tests

summaries: Tests should clearly communicate what behavior they verify.

data.description: == == compares object identity (same memory address), not content. Always use .equals() .equals() for String String, Integer Integer, and other objects. Be aware of null: use Objects.equals(a, b) Objects.equals(a, b) to handle nulls safely. For collections, use .equals() .equals() as well. Exception: enums can use == == because there's only one instance of each enum value.
data.text: Don't use == == for object equality; use .equals() .equals()
data.title: Don't use == == for object equality; use .equals() .equals()

summaries: Always use .equals() .equals() to compare object content, not == ==.

data.description: If you override equals() equals(), you must override hashCode() hashCode() such that equal objects have the same hash code. This is required for correct behavior in HashMap HashMap, HashSet HashSet, etc. Use Objects.hash() Objects.hash() for a simple implementation. Modern IDEs can generate both methods correctly. Records automatically provide correct equals() equals() and hashCode() hashCode().
data.text: Override hashCode() hashCode() when you override equals() equals()
data.title: Override hashCode() hashCode() when you override equals() equals()

summaries: These methods must be consistent to work correctly in collections.

data.description: Modern C# offers concise and expressive constructs: file-scoped namespaces (C# 10+), collection expressions (C# 12+), pattern matching, record types, init-only properties, required members, global usings, switch expressions, and target-typed new expressions. Use them when they make code clearer and better aligned with the current .NET ecosystem. For example, use List<int> numbers = [1, 2, 3]; List<int> numbers = [1, 2, 3]; instead of new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 } new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 } in C# 12+. These features reduce ceremony and improve signal-to-noise ratio.
data.text: Use modern C# conventions and language features
data.title: Use modern C# conventions and language features

summaries: Prefer current C# language constructs when they improve readability and correctness.

data.description: In C# 10+, use file-scoped namespace declarations to reduce indentation: namespace MyApp.Services; namespace MyApp.Services; instead of wrapping the entire file in a block. This saves horizontal space and keeps code at lower indentation levels. Use this consistently across a project for all files with a single namespace.
data.text: Use file-scoped namespaces to reduce indentation
data.title: Use file-scoped namespaces to reduce indentation

summaries: File-scoped namespaces eliminate one level of nesting.

data.description: When the type is specified on the left, use new() new() on the right: List<string> names = new(); List<string> names = new(); instead of new List<string>() new List<string>(). This reduces redundancy without losing clarity. Don't use it when the type isn't obvious from context. This feature works for object creation, field/property initialization, and local variables.
data.text: Use target-typed new when the type is obvious
data.title: Use target-typed new when the type is obvious

summaries: Omit the type on the right side when it's clear from the left.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Type Usage and Variables
data.description: Use var var when the type is clear from the right-hand side: var customer = new Customer(); var customer = new Customer(); or var count = customers.Count; var count = customers.Count;. Avoid var var when the type is not obvious: prefer explicit types for method returns, complex expressions, or when clarity matters. The goal is to reduce noise without reducing understanding. Teams should agree on a consistent style.
data.text: Use var var only when the type is obvious
data.title: Use var var only when the type is obvious

summaries: Implicit typing should help readability, not hide intent.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Type Usage and Variables
data.description: Use descriptive names that explain intent: orderTotal orderTotal not temp temp, activeUsers activeUsers not list list. Avoid single-letter names except for tight loops or lambda parameters. Names should make the code readable without comments. For locals, use camelCase; for fields, use _camelCase (with underscore prefix for private fields).
data.text: Prefer meaningful variable names over comments
data.title: Prefer meaningful variable names over comments

summaries: Variable names should be self-documenting.

data.description: Enable nullable reference types (<Nullable>enable</Nullable> <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in .csproj) to make nullability explicit in APIs and implementations. Use string? string? for nullable strings, string string for non-null strings. This reduces null-related bugs and makes method contracts clearer. Use ! ! (null-forgiving operator) sparingly and only when you're certain a value isn't null but the compiler can't prove it. Prefer explicit null checks instead.
data.text: Use nullable reference types and explicit null handling
data.title: Use nullable reference types and explicit null handling

summaries: Nullability should be part of the contract, not an afterthought.

data.description: Use ?? ?? for default values: name = input ?? "default" name = input ?? "default". Use ?. ?. for safe member access: length = person?.Name?.Length length = person?.Name?.Length. Use ??= ??= for lazy initialization: _cache ??= new Dictionary<string, string>() _cache ??= new Dictionary<string, string>(). These operators are more concise and expressive than explicit null checks. Don't chain them excessively; if the logic gets complex, use explicit if statements.
data.text: Use null coalescing and conditional operators idiomatically
data.title: Use null coalescing and conditional operators idiomatically

summaries: C# has concise operators for null handling that improve readability.

data.description: Use using using for IDisposable resources and await using await using for IAsyncDisposable resources. Prefer the simplified using declaration syntax (C# 8+): using var stream = File.OpenRead(path); using var stream = File.OpenRead(path); which disposes at the end of the enclosing scope. This is more reliable than manual cleanup and makes intent obvious. Never forget to dispose resources like streams, database connections, or HTTP clients that wrap connections.
data.text: Prefer using using statements and async cleanup
data.title: Prefer using using statements and async cleanup

summaries: Resource lifetime should be clear and deterministic.

data.description: Use async async and await await for I/O-bound work such as network calls, file access, database operations. Return Task Task or Task<T> Task<T> from async methods. Name async methods with an Async Async suffix (e.g., GetDataAsync GetDataAsync). Never block on async code with .Result .Result or .Wait() .Wait() in production code—this can cause deadlocks, especially in UI or ASP.NET contexts. If you must block (e.g., in Main), use .GetAwaiter().GetResult() .GetAwaiter().GetResult() which has better exception semantics.
data.text: Prefer async/await for I/O-bound operations
data.title: Prefer async/await for I/O-bound operations

summaries: Asynchronous workflows should be expressed with the language's native async model.

data.description: async void async void methods cannot be awaited and make error handling difficult (exceptions crash the process or get lost). Use async Task async Task instead. The only exception is event handlers, which are required to be void by the event signature. For fire-and-forget scenarios, consider returning Task and explicitly ignoring it at the call site with a comment explaining why.
data.text: Avoid async void except for event handlers
data.title: Avoid async void except for event handlers

summaries: Async methods should return Task or Task<T> so callers can await them.

data.description: In library code (not UI or ASP.NET request handlers), use await operation.ConfigureAwait(false) await operation.ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid capturing the synchronization context. This improves performance and prevents deadlocks. In application code (UI, ASP.NET), omit ConfigureAwait or use ConfigureAwait(true) to stay on the original context. Know the difference; incorrect use can cause bugs.
data.text: Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
data.title: Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code

summaries: Libraries shouldn't capture the synchronization context unnecessarily.

data.description: Don't mark methods async if they only do CPU-bound work. Use Task.Run(() => CpuBoundWork()) Task.Run(() => CpuBoundWork()) to run CPU-bound operations on a thread pool thread. Async/await is designed for I/O-bound asynchrony where threads can be released while waiting. For CPU-bound parallelism, use Task Parallel Library (TPL) or Parallel LINQ. Mixing them incorrectly hurts performance.
data.text: Don't use async for CPU-bound work
data.title: Don't use async for CPU-bound work

summaries: Async/await is for I/O-bound work; use Task.Run for CPU-bound parallelism.

data.description: LINQ is powerful for querying collections, but long chains of transformations can become hard to read. Use it where it improves readability and expressiveness. Break complex queries into steps with intermediate variables. Use method syntax for simple queries (.Where() .Where(), .Select() .Select()) and query syntax when readability improves (joins, grouping). If a query becomes difficult to follow, prefer a more explicit loop or helper method.
data.text: Use LINQ and expression-based patterns carefully
data.title: Use LINQ and expression-based patterns carefully

summaries: Compact expressions should improve clarity without becoming opaque.

data.description: LINQ queries using Where Where, Select Select, OrderBy OrderBy, etc. use deferred execution—they don't run until you enumerate the result (foreach, ToList, ToArray, Count, etc.). This can cause subtle bugs if the underlying collection changes or if you enumerate multiple times (re-executing the query). Use .ToList() .ToList() or .ToArray() .ToArray() if you need to materialize the result immediately or enumerate multiple times.
data.text: Understand deferred execution in LINQ
data.title: Understand deferred execution in LINQ

summaries: Many LINQ operations are lazy and execute only when enumerated.

data.description: Use collection initializers: var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }; var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };. In C# 12+, use collection expressions: List<int> numbers = [1, 2, 3]; List<int> numbers = [1, 2, 3];. These are more concise than repeatedly calling .Add() .Add(). For dictionaries, use: new Dictionary<string, int> { ["key"] = value } new Dictionary<string, int> { ["key"] = value } or dictionary initializer syntax.
data.text: Prefer collection initializers and collection expressions
data.title: Prefer collection initializers and collection expressions

summaries: Use concise syntax for initializing collections.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Pattern Matching and Switch Expressions
data.description: Use pattern matching instead of as as followed by null checks: if (obj is Customer customer) if (obj is Customer customer) instead of var customer = obj as Customer; if (customer != null) var customer = obj as Customer; if (customer != null). Use switch expressions for exhaustive matching on types or values. Use property patterns to match on object members: if (order is { Status: "Pending", Total: > 100 }) if (order is { Status: "Pending", Total: > 100 }). This reduces boilerplate and makes intent clearer.
data.text: Use pattern matching to reduce casting and null checks
data.title: Use pattern matching to reduce casting and null checks

summaries: Pattern matching makes type checks and data extraction more concise.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Pattern Matching and Switch Expressions
data.description: Switch expressions (var result = value switch { ... } var result = value switch { ... }) are often clearer than switch statements because they must return a value and the compiler enforces exhaustiveness with a discard pattern _ _. Use them for mapping values or pattern matching. Use traditional switch statements for imperative flows with side effects.
data.text: Prefer switch expressions over switch statements
data.title: Prefer switch expressions over switch statements

summaries: Switch expressions are more concise and enforce exhaustiveness.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Record Types and Immutability
data.description: Use record record or record struct record struct for DTOs, value objects, and immutable data carriers. Records automatically generate value-based Equals Equals, GetHashCode GetHashCode, and ToString ToString.
