Use positional syntax for simple records: public record Person(string Name, int Age); public record Person(string Name, int Age);. Use nominal syntax for complex records with additional members. Records support with-expressions for non-destructive mutation.
data.text: Use record types for immutable data objects
data.title: Use record types for immutable data objects

summaries: Records provide value-based equality and concise syntax for immutable data.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Record Types and Immutability
data.description: Use init init instead of set set to make properties settable only during object initialization: public string Name { get; init; } public string Name { get; init; }. This works with object initializers and provides a middle ground between mutable and fully immutable objects. Use required required modifier (C# 11+) to enforce that a property must be set during initialization: public required string Name { get; init; } public required string Name { get; init; }.
data.text: Use init-only properties for immutability
data.title: Use init-only properties for immutability

summaries: Init-only setters allow object initialization but prevent later mutation.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Dependency Injection and Architecture
data.description: C# systems are easier to test and evolve when dependencies are explicit and injected (constructor injection is preferred) rather than hidden in static singletons or global state. Use the built-in DI container in ASP.NET Core or a third-party container. Register services with appropriate lifetimes (Singleton, Scoped, Transient). Clear dependency boundaries make code easier to reason about and less tightly coupled.
data.text: Favor dependency injection and explicit dependencies
data.title: Favor dependency injection and explicit dependencies

summaries: Components should declare what they depend on instead of hiding it in global state.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/C#/Dependency Injection and Architecture
data.description: Injecting IServiceProvider IServiceProvider and calling GetService<T>() GetService<T>() hides dependencies and makes testing harder. It's a service locator anti-pattern. Prefer explicit constructor injection. Exception: framework code or plugins where types aren't known at compile time. Even then, consider using factory patterns instead.
data.text: Avoid service locator anti-pattern
data.title: Avoid service locator anti-pattern

summaries: Don't inject IServiceProvider to resolve dependencies dynamically.

data.description: .NET design guidance favors intuitive naming (nouns for classes, verbs for methods), consistent behavior, and clear contracts. Use PascalCase for public members, prefix interfaces with I I, suffix exception types with Exception Exception. Public APIs should provide predictable failure semantics (throw exceptions for errors, return null/empty for "not found"). Avoid surprising defaults. Use overloads thoughtfully. Document pre/post conditions.
data.text: Keep APIs consistent with .NET design guidelines
data.title: Keep APIs consistent with .NET design guidelines

summaries: Public APIs should be easy to discover, use, and evolve.

data.description: Use properties (public string Name { get; set; } public string Name { get; set; }) instead of getter/setter methods. Properties are semantically cleaner and work with features like object initializers, expression-bodied members, and data binding. Use methods for operations that do significant work, have side effects, or take parameters. If getting a value is expensive or can throw, use a method instead.
data.text: Prefer properties over getter methods for data access
data.title: Prefer properties over getter methods for data access

summaries: Properties are the idiomatic way to expose data in C#.

data.description: Don't use exceptions for normal control flow. For example, use TryParse TryParse instead of catching parse exceptions. Exceptions should represent truly exceptional situations: invalid input, resource exhaustion, network failures. Use return values, out parameters, or result types for expected failure paths. This improves performance and makes the code intent clearer.
data.text: Use exceptions for exceptional conditions, not flow control
data.title: Use exceptions for exceptional conditions, not flow control

summaries: Exceptions are expensive and should represent errors, not expected conditions.

data.description: Catch specific exception types, not general Exception Exception. Don't swallow exceptions silently (empty catch). When rethrowing, use throw; throw; not throw ex; throw ex; to preserve the stack trace. When wrapping exceptions, use InnerException InnerException to chain them. Add context to exceptions when rethrowing: throw new ApplicationException("Failed to process order", ex) throw new ApplicationException("Failed to process order", ex). Log exceptions at the right boundary (usually near the top of the call stack).
data.text: Catch specific exceptions and preserve context
data.title: Catch specific exceptions and preserve context

summaries: Exception handling should be precise and informative.

data.description: Use descriptive test method names that explain what is being tested and the expected outcome (e.g., WhenOrderIsEmpty_TotalShouldBeZero WhenOrderIsEmpty_TotalShouldBeZero). Follow Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. One logical assertion per test. Tests should be independent, fast, and deterministic. Use mocking frameworks sparingly; prefer real objects when practical. Test behavior, not implementation details.
data.text: Write clear, focused unit tests
data.title: Write clear, focused unit tests

summaries: Tests should clearly document expected behavior.

data.description: Never use .ToLower() == .ToLower() .ToLower() == .ToLower() for case-insensitive comparison. Use string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) or .Equals(..., StringComparison.CurrentCultureIgnoreCase) .Equals(..., StringComparison.CurrentCultureIgnoreCase). This is more correct, more efficient, and handles cultures properly. == == uses ordinal comparison which may not be what you want for internationalized text.
data.text: Don't compare strings with == for case-insensitive comparison
data.title: Don't compare strings with == for case-insensitive comparison

summaries: Use StringComparison enum for proper string comparison.

data.description: Value types (structs, primitives) are copied when passed around; reference types (classes) are passed by reference. Structs should be small and immutable. Boxing occurs when a value type is converted to object object or an interface—this allocates heap memory and hurts performance. Use generic collections (List<int> List<int>) instead of non-generic ones (ArrayList ArrayList) to avoid boxing.
data.text: Understand value vs reference types and boxing
data.title: Understand value vs reference types and boxing

summaries: Structs are value types; classes are reference types. Boxing has performance implications.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Ownership and Memory Safety
data.description: The central Rust pattern is to model data ownership explicitly and allow the compiler to enforce safety. Prefer borrowing (&T &T, &mut T &mut T) over unnecessary cloning. Make lifetimes and mutation boundaries clear through the type system. Code that works with ownership idiomatically is easier to reason about, more efficient, and prevents entire classes of bugs (use-after-free, double-free, data races). When the borrow checker complains, the solution is usually to clarify ownership, not to add more lifetime parameters.
data.text: Embrace ownership and borrowing as the primary design model
data.title: Embrace ownership and borrowing as the primary design model

summaries: Rust code should be structured around ownership rules rather than fighting them.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Ownership and Memory Safety
data.description: Functions should accept &T &T or &mut T &mut T when they don't need to own the data. Reserve cloning (clone() clone()) for cases where you truly need an independent copy. Borrowing is zero-cost; cloning can be expensive. If your function signature requires T T (owned value), consider whether &T &T would work. Immutable borrows (&T &T) can be shared; mutable borrows (&mut T &mut T) are exclusive.
data.text: Prefer borrowing over cloning for performance
data.title: Prefer borrowing over cloning for performance

summaries: Pass references when you don't need ownership.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Ownership and Memory Safety
data.description: Use Box<T> Box<T> for heap allocation and owned data. Use Rc<T> Rc<T> for shared ownership in single-threaded contexts. Use Arc<T> Arc<T> for shared ownership across threads. Use RefCell<T> RefCell<T> for interior mutability (runtime borrow checking) when compile-time checks are too restrictive. Use Mutex<T> Mutex<T> or RwLock<T> RwLock<T> for thread-safe interior mutability. Each has trade-offs; understand when to use which. Prefer simple ownership when possible.
data.text: Use smart pointers intentionally for shared ownership
data.title: Use smart pointers intentionally for shared ownership

summaries: Rc, Arc, Box, and RefCell solve specific ownership patterns.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Ownership and Memory Safety
data.description: Rust's compiler usually infers lifetimes automatically (lifetime elision rules). Explicit lifetime annotations are needed when the compiler can't determine relationships. Lifetimes aren't about "managing memory"—they're about expressing borrowing relationships. If you find yourself fighting lifetimes, step back and reconsider whether ownership or cloning would simplify the design. Most Rust code has very few explicit lifetimes.
data.text: Understand lifetimes as borrowing constraints, not complexity
data.title: Understand lifetimes as borrowing constraints, not complexity

summaries: Lifetimes document how long references remain valid; they usually can be inferred.

data.description: Rust code should favor Result<T, E> Result<T, E> for recoverable errors and Option<T> Option<T> for optional values. These types force callers to handle errors explicitly. The ? ? operator propagates errors concisely. Use unwrap() unwrap() and expect() expect() only in prototypes, tests, or when failure is truly impossible (and document why). In library code, always return Results so callers can handle errors appropriately. Custom error types should implement std::error::Error std::error::Error.
data.text: Use Result Result and Option Option instead of ad hoc error flags
data.title: Use Result Result and Option Option instead of ad hoc error flags

summaries: Failure handling should be explicit and typed.

data.description: ? ? automatically converts errors (via From From trait) and returns early if the result is Err Err. It's equivalent to match result { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(e.into()) } match result { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(e.into()) }. This keeps happy-path code clean while preserving explicit error propagation. Use it liberally in functions returning Result Result. It works with Option Option too (returns early on None None).
data.text: Use ? ? operator for clean error propagation
data.title: Use ? ? operator for clean error propagation

summaries: The ? ? operator makes error handling concise without hiding it.

data.description: Library functions should return Result Result for errors that callers might want to handle. Panic only for programmer errors (contract violations, unreachable code paths) where recovery isn't meaningful. Use panic! panic!, unreachable! unreachable!, and unimplemented! unimplemented! sparingly. Document panic conditions in function documentation. In application code, panics are more acceptable but should still be deliberate.
data.text: Avoid panicking in library code; return Results instead
data.title: Avoid panicking in library code; return Results instead

summaries: Panics should be reserved for truly unrecoverable bugs, not errors.

data.description: Custom error types should implement std::error::Error std::error::Error, Display Display, and Debug Debug. Use enums to represent multiple error cases. Consider using crates like thiserror thiserror to reduce boilerplate. Implement From From to enable automatic error conversions with ? ?. Provide context: error messages should help users understand what went wrong and why.
data.text: Design error types that compose well
data.title: Design error types that compose well

summaries: Error types should be informative and work with ? ? and From From conversions.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Pattern Matching and Control Flow
data.description: Rust makes match match a first-class tool for expressing decision logic. Use match match for exhaustive matching on enums, structs, and tuples. Use if let if let for matching a single pattern when you don't care about other cases. Pattern matching is more than a switch statement—it destructures data and enforces exhaustiveness. This is especially useful for enums, option values, and state machines. Prefer matching over boolean chains when you have structured data.
data.text: Prefer pattern matching over imperative branching when it improves clarity
data.title: Prefer pattern matching over imperative branching when it improves clarity

summaries: Enums and structured data should be handled with pattern matching.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Pattern Matching and Control Flow
data.description: Design types so that invalid states can't be constructed. For example, use enums instead of booleans to represent states. Use newtypes (tuple structs) to distinguish semantically different values of the same underlying type (e.g., struct Meters(f64) struct Meters(f64) vs struct Seconds(f64) struct Seconds(f64)). Use Option Option instead of sentinel values (like -1). The compiler will prevent misuse at compile time, eliminating entire classes of bugs.
data.text: Make illegal states unrepresentable with type design
data.title: Make illegal states unrepresentable with type design

summaries: Use the type system to encode invariants and prevent invalid states.

data.description: Rust API design should emphasize clarity, minimal surprise, and ergonomic use. Follow naming conventions: types are PascalCase PascalCase, functions and variables are snake_case snake_case, constants are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, lifetimes are 'lowercase 'lowercase. Prefer small, composable abstractions. Avoid unnecessarily complex generic signatures. Good Rust APIs let common usage be obvious and make advanced cases possible without friction. Don't over-genericize unless it provides real value.
data.text: Keep APIs ergonomic and minimal
data.title: Keep APIs ergonomic and minimal

summaries: Rust APIs should be easy to use and hard to misuse.

data.description: Method names should follow conventions: .iter() .iter() for iterators, .into_*() .into_*() for consuming conversions, .to_*() .to_*() for copying conversions, .as_*() .as_*() for cheap reference-to-reference conversions. Getters don't use get_ get_ prefix (just name() name(), not get_name() get_name()). Mutable methods use *_mut *_mut suffix. Constructors are new() new(), fallible constructors return Result Result. Boolean queries use is_ is_ or has_ has_ prefix. These conventions make APIs predictable.
data.text: Follow naming conventions and standard patterns
data.title: Follow naming conventions and standard patterns

summaries: Rust has strong conventions that improve consistency across the ecosystem.

data.description: Rust's design goal is "zero-cost abstractions": high-level code should compile to the same machine code as low-level code. Prefer generics over trait objects when performance matters. Use impl Trait impl Trait for return types to avoid heap allocation. Avoid unnecessary boxing or dynamic dispatch. Use #[inline] #[inline] for small, hot functions. Design APIs so the compiler can optimize aggressively.
data.text: Design for zero-cost abstractions
data.title: Design for zero-cost abstractions

summaries: APIs should avoid runtime overhead when possible.

data.description: Instead of &String &String, accept &str &str. Instead of &Vec<T> &Vec<T>, accept &[T] &[T]. Instead of &Box<T> &Box<T>, accept &T &T. This makes APIs more flexible: they work with owned types, borrowed types, and string/vector literals. Callers can pass more types without conversion. Exception: when you need the specific functionality of the owned type.
data.text: Accept borrowed types for flexibility
data.title: Accept borrowed types for flexibility

summaries: Function parameters should accept the most general borrowed form.

data.description: Iterators are a core part of Rust style and often produce clearer, more efficient code than manually managing indices or temporary collections. Use .iter() .iter(), .iter_mut() .iter_mut(), and .into_iter() .into_iter() appropriately. Chain iterator adaptors (.map() .map(), .filter() .filter(), .fold() .fold(), .collect() .collect()) to express transformations functionally. Iterators are lazy and zero-cost. If a loop is more readable, that's still valid. Don't force iterator chains that obscure intent.
data.text: Prefer iterators and collection methods over manual loops when they are clearer
data.title: Prefer iterators and collection methods over manual loops when they are clearer

summaries: Idiomatic Rust uses iterator pipelines for transformation and filtering.

data.description: .iter() .iter() iterates over immutable references (&T &T), .iter_mut() .iter_mut() over mutable references (&mut T &mut T), .into_iter() .into_iter() consumes the collection and yields owned values (T T). For loops use into_iter() into_iter() by default; collections implement IntoIterator IntoIterator differently depending on whether they're borrowed or owned. Understanding this prevents ownership bugs.
data.text: Understand when iterators consume and when they borrow
data.title: Understand when iterators consume and when they borrow

summaries: Know the difference between iter(), iter_mut(), and into_iter().

data.description: .collect() .collect() can produce any type that implements FromIterator FromIterator. Usually the type is inferred, but sometimes you need to annotate: let vec: Vec<_> = iter.collect(); let vec: Vec<_> = iter.collect(); or use turbofish syntax: iter.collect::<Vec<_>>() iter.collect::<Vec<_>>(). The _ _ lets Rust infer the element type while you specify the collection type.
data.text: Collect iterators with type annotations when needed
data.title: Collect iterators with type annotations when needed

summaries: .collect() .collect() can produce many types; sometimes you must specify which.

data.description: Derive Debug Debug for all public types to enable debugging. Implement Display Display for user-facing output. Derive Clone Clone if cloning is meaningful, Copy Copy if the type is small and bitwise-copyable. Implement PartialEq PartialEq and Eq Eq for equality, PartialOrd PartialOrd and Ord Ord for ordering. These standard traits integrate your types with the ecosystem. Use #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] liberally.
data.text: Implement standard traits for your types
data.title: Implement standard traits for your types

summaries: Deriving or implementing Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq makes types more usable.

data.description: Use where where clauses for complex bounds to keep signatures readable. Only require the traits you actually use. Overly generic code can be hard to understand; sometimes concrete types are better. Use impl Trait impl Trait for input parameters (fn foo(x: impl Display) fn foo(x: impl Display)) when you don't need to name the type. Use it for return types to hide implementation details and improve compilation time.
data.text: Use trait bounds to express requirements clearly
data.title: Use trait bounds to express requirements clearly

summaries: Generic parameters should have minimal, precise bounds.

data.description: Use modules (mod mod) to organize code logically. Keep types, functions, and traits that work together in the same module. Use pub pub to export public APIs, leave internal helpers private. Use pub(crate) pub(crate) for items that should be public within the crate but not outside. Use re-exports (pub use pub use) in lib.rs to create a clean public API. Good module design makes the crate easy to navigate and understand.
data.text: Design module hierarchies that reflect usage patterns
data.title: Design module hierarchies that reflect usage patterns

summaries: Modules should group related functionality and control visibility.

data.description: Users should be able to import what they need with short paths. Re-export important types at the crate root or high-level modules. For example, if crate::foo::bar::Thing crate::foo::bar::Thing is commonly used, re-export it as crate::Thing crate::Thing. Avoid forcing users to navigate deep hierarchies for common APIs.
data.text: Prefer flat, intuitive module structures
data.title: Prefer flat, intuitive module structures

summaries: Avoid deep nesting; keep common items easy to import.

data.description: Rust's Send Send and Sync Sync marker traits ensure that only thread-safe types can be shared across threads. This prevents data races at compile time. Use Arc Arc for shared ownership across threads, Mutex Mutex/RwLock RwLock for shared mutable state. Use channels (std::sync::mpsc std::sync::mpsc or crossbeam_channel crossbeam_channel) for message passing between threads. Rust makes concurrency much safer than in most languages.
data.text: Leverage Rust's fearless concurrency guarantees
data.title: Leverage Rust's fearless concurrency guarantees

summaries: The type system prevents data races at compile time.

data.description: When possible, structure concurrent programs so threads communicate by sending messages (channels) rather than sharing memory. This reduces the need for locks and makes the program easier to reason about. Use mpsc::channel() mpsc::channel() for asynchronous communication. Reserve shared mutable state (behind Mutex Mutex/RwLock RwLock) for cases where it truly simplifies the design.
data.text: Prefer message passing over shared mutable state
data.title: Prefer message passing over shared mutable state

summaries: Channels and message passing reduce coupling and prevent races.

data.description: Every public function, type, and module should have a doc comment (/// ///). Explain what the item does, when to use it, and any important behavior. Include examples in doc comments—they're executable as tests (via cargo test cargo test). Use //! //! for module-level documentation. Good docs make your crate easier to use and maintain. Run cargo doc --open cargo doc --open to preview.
data.text: Write comprehensive documentation with examples
data.title: Write comprehensive documentation with examples

summaries: Public items should have doc comments with usage examples.

data.description: Rust supports unit tests naturally with #[cfg(test)] mod tests #[cfg(test)] mod tests at the bottom of each file. Keep tests close to the code they exercise. Write integration tests in the tests/ tests/ directory for public API validation. Use #[test] #[test] for test functions. Use assert! assert!, assert_eq! assert_eq!, and assert_ne! assert_ne! for assertions. Test edge cases, error paths, and invariants. Tests are documentation of expected behavior.
data.text: Write unit tests alongside the code they validate
data.title: Write unit tests alongside the code they validate

summaries: Rust makes it easy to keep tests close to implementation.

data.description: Run cargo fmt cargo fmt to standardize formatting automatically (uses rustfmt). Run cargo clippy cargo clippy to surface common mistakes, anti-patterns, and performance issues (Clippy has hundreds of lints). These tools reduce style churn, encourage consistency, and help developers focus on architecture and correctness. Make them part of CI. Use rustfmt.toml rustfmt.toml and .clippy.toml .clippy.toml for project-specific configuration.
data.text: Use cargo fmt and clippy as part of the normal workflow
data.title: Use cargo fmt and clippy as part of the normal workflow

summaries: Tooling should enforce style and catch common issues automatically.

data.description: Clippy suggests improvements for correctness, performance, and idiomaticity. Don't ignore its warnings blindly; understand why it's suggesting a change. Most suggestions make code better. You can disable specific lints with #[allow(clippy::lint_name)] #[allow(clippy::lint_name)] when you have a good reason, but document why. Clippy helps you write more idiomatic Rust.
data.text: Run clippy regularly and understand its suggestions
data.title: Run clippy regularly and understand its suggestions

summaries: Clippy lints represent accumulated community wisdom.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Common Patterns and Anti-Patterns
data.description: Wrap primitive types (like u64 u64, String String) in newtypes to make invalid operations impossible. For example, struct UserId(u64) struct UserId(u64) prevents mixing user IDs with order IDs. Newtypes are zero-cost at runtime (single-element tuple structs are optimized away). This prevents bugs at compile time and makes APIs clearer.
data.text: Use the newtype pattern for type safety
data.title: Use the newtype pattern for type safety

summaries: Wrap primitive types in tuple structs to prevent misuse.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Common Patterns and Anti-Patterns
data.description: When a type has many optional fields, use the builder pattern instead of multiple constructors. The builder lets callers specify only the fields they care about. Example: Config::builder().timeout(30).retries(3).build() Config::builder().timeout(30).retries(3).build(). Libraries like typed-builder typed-builder can generate builders automatically. This is more ergonomic than constructors with many optional parameters.
data.text: Use builder pattern for complex construction
data.title: Use builder pattern for complex construction

summaries: Builders make objects with many optional parameters easier to construct.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Common Patterns and Anti-Patterns
data.description: Instead of accepting &str &str with values like "json" or "xml", define an enum: enum Format { Json, Xml } enum Format { Json, Xml }. This prevents typos, enables exhaustive matching, and makes the API self-documenting. Use strings only when the set of values is truly open-ended.
data.text: Avoid stringly-typed APIs; use enums
data.title: Avoid stringly-typed APIs; use enums

summaries: Don't use strings for values that have a fixed set of options.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Rust/Common Patterns and Anti-Patterns
data.description: Cloning is often used as a quick fix when the borrow checker complains, but excessive cloning hurts performance and hides design issues. If you find yourself cloning frequently, step back and reconsider your ownership model. Sometimes you need shared ownership (Rc Rc/Arc Arc), sometimes you need to restructure the code, sometimes lifetime parameters help. Cloning should be deliberate, not a workaround.
data.text: Don't clone unnecessarily to appease the borrow checker
data.title: Don't clone unnecessarily to appease the borrow checker

summaries: If you're cloning a lot, your ownership design may need refinement.

data.description: Unsafe code opts out of Rust's safety guarantees and must be carefully reviewed. Use it only when necessary (FFI, low-level optimizations, certain data structures). Encapsulate unsafe code in safe APIs. Document invariants that must be maintained. Minimize the unsafe surface area. Most Rust programs have zero unsafe blocks; most libraries have only a few carefully audited ones.
data.text: Avoid unsafe except when absolutely necessary
data.title: Avoid unsafe except when absolutely necessary

summaries: Unsafe code should be rare, encapsulated, and well-documented.

data.description: Use // SAFETY: // SAFETY: comments to explain why each unsafe block upholds Rust's safety guarantees. What invariants must hold? What could go wrong? How do you prevent it? This makes code review possible and prevents bugs when the code changes. Treat unsafe code with extreme care; it's where memory safety bugs can occur.
data.text: Document safety invariants clearly
data.title: Document safety invariants clearly

summaries: Every unsafe block must explain why it's safe.

data.description: Python values readability above almost all else. Follow PEP 8 for layout and naming: 4 spaces per indentation level (never tabs), 79-100 character line length, two blank lines between top-level definitions, one blank line between methods. The Zen of Python (import this import this) guides design: "Explicit is better than implicit," "Simple is better than complex," "Readability counts." Code should be easy to scan and understand by the next person who reads it.
data.text: Follow PEP 8 and the Zen of Python
data.title: Follow PEP 8 and the Zen of Python

summaries: Python code should be readable first and visually consistent.

data.description: When faced with multiple ways to solve a problem, prefer the most obvious and readable one. Python's design encourages consistency. For example, use with with for resource management, list comprehensions for simple transformations, is is for singleton comparisons. This philosophy makes Python codebases easier to understand across different teams.
data.text: There should be one obvious way to do it
data.title: There should be one obvious way to do it

summaries: Python prefers a single, clear idiom over many equivalent approaches.

data.description: Use snake_case snake_case for functions, variables, and module names. Use CapWords CapWords (PascalCase) for class names. Use UPPER_CASE UPPER_CASE for constants. Prefer descriptive names: calculate_total_price() calculate_total_price() not calc() calc(). Functions should do one thing well and fit on a screen. Short, focused functions are easier to test, reuse, and understand. Avoid single-letter names except for narrow scopes (loop counters, lambda parameters).
data.text: Use descriptive snake_case names and keep functions short
data.title: Use descriptive snake_case names and keep functions short

summaries: Names should communicate intent and functions should stay focused.

data.description: Prefix internal functions, methods, and variables with a single underscore (_helper _helper) to indicate they're not part of the public API. Use double underscores (__private __private) sparingly—it triggers name mangling to avoid name conflicts in subclasses. Don't use trailing underscores except to avoid keyword conflicts (class_ class_ when class class is a keyword). _ _ alone is used for throwaway variables in loops or unpacking.
data.text: Use leading underscores for internal implementation
data.title: Use leading underscores for internal implementation

summaries: Single underscore indicates internal use; double underscore triggers name mangling.

data.description: Group imports in this order, separated by blank lines: (1) standard library imports, (2) third-party library imports, (3) local application imports. Within each group, sort alphabetically. Use absolute imports for clarity. Avoid wildcard imports (from module import * from module import *) as they pollute the namespace. Use from module import specific_name from module import specific_name when you frequently use specific names.
data.text: Organize imports in standard order
data.title: Organize imports in standard order

summaries: Standard library, third-party, local imports, each group alphabetically.

data.description: If two modules import each other, the design likely needs improvement. Extract shared code to a third module, use dependency injection, or import inside functions (as a last resort). Circular imports cause cryptic errors and suggest tight coupling. Refactoring to eliminate them usually improves design.
data.text: Avoid circular imports through better module design
data.title: Avoid circular imports through better module design

summaries: Circular imports indicate coupling that should be refactored.

data.description: Never use mutable objects as default arguments: def foo(items=[]) def foo(items=[]) is wrong. The default is created once at function definition and shared across all calls. Use None None and initialize inside: def foo(items=None): items = items or [] def foo(items=None): items = items or []. This is one of Python's most common gotchas. Immutable defaults (numbers, strings, tuples, None None) are safe.
data.text: Avoid mutable default arguments
data.title: Avoid mutable default arguments

summaries: Mutable defaults like [] [] or {} {} are shared across calls, causing bugs.

data.description: Use *args *args to accept any number of positional arguments, **kwargs **kwargs for any keyword arguments. This is useful for wrappers, decorators, and extensible APIs. Example: def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return func(*args, **kwargs) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return func(*args, **kwargs). Be careful not to overuse; explicit parameters are clearer when you know what you need.
data.text: Use *args *args and **kwargs **kwargs for flexible APIs
data.title: Use *args *args and **kwargs **kwargs for flexible APIs

summaries: Variadic arguments make functions extensible without breaking callers.

data.description: For functions with multiple parameters, especially booleans or similar types, use keyword arguments at the call site: send_email(to=user, subject="Hello", urgent=True) send_email(to=user, subject="Hello", urgent=True) is clearer than send_email(user, "Hello", True) send_email(user, "Hello", True). You can enforce keyword-only arguments with * *: def foo(arg1, *, kwonly) def foo(arg1, *, kwonly) makes kwonly kwonly keyword-only.
data.text: Prefer keyword arguments for clarity
data.title: Prefer keyword arguments for clarity

summaries: Keyword arguments make call sites self-documenting.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Data Structures and Idioms
data.description: Use list comprehensions for simple mappings and filtering: [x*2 for x in items if x > 0] [x*2 for x in items if x > 0]. Use generator expressions for lazy evaluation: (x*2 for x in items) (x*2 for x in items). Don't nest more than two levels or make them too complex. If the comprehension is hard to read, use a regular loop. Comprehensions should improve clarity, not obscure it.
data.text: Use list comprehensions and generator expressions idiomatically
data.title: Use list comprehensions and generator expressions idiomatically

summaries: Comprehensions are concise for simple transformations; avoid complexity.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Data Structures and Idioms
data.description: For small structured data, use @dataclass @dataclass (Python 3.7+) or NamedTuple NamedTuple rather than elaborate custom classes. Dataclasses generate __init__ __init__, __repr__ __repr__, and __eq__ __eq__ automatically. For simple cases, dictionaries are fine. Don't create heavyweight class hierarchies for simple data. Keep it simple and Pythonic.
data.text: Prefer dataclasses and plain data structures for simple models
data.title: Prefer dataclasses and plain data structures for simple models

summaries: Simple data containers should be expressed directly rather than over-engineered.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Data Structures and Idioms
data.description: Lists ([] []) for ordered, mutable sequences. Tuples (() ()) for immutable sequences, often used for heterogeneous data. Sets ({} {} or set() set()) for unique, unordered collections with fast membership tests. Dicts ({} {}) for key-value mappings. Use sets for membership testing, deduplication, and set operations. Don't use lists when you mean sets. Know the time complexities: list append is O(1), list insert is O(n); set/dict lookup is O(1) average.
data.text: Understand when to use lists, tuples, sets, and dicts
data.title: Understand when to use lists, tuples, sets, and dicts

summaries: Choose the right data structure for the use case.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Context Managers and Resources
data.description: Always use with with statements for resources: with open(filename) as f: with open(filename) as f: ensures the file is closed even if an exception occurs. This works for files, locks, database connections, network sockets—anything implementing the context manager protocol (__enter__ __enter__/__exit__ __exit__). Never manually open and close resources without good reason; with with is the idiomatic way.
data.text: Use context managers for resources
data.title: Use context managers for resources

summaries: Files and other resources should be managed deterministically with with with.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Context Managers and Resources
data.description: Use contextlib.contextmanager contextlib.contextmanager decorator to create simple context managers with generator functions. Use classes with __enter__ __enter__ and __exit__ __exit__ for more complex cases. Context managers are great for temporary state changes, acquiring and releasing locks, timing blocks, transaction management. The pattern makes resource management explicit and exception-safe.
data.text: Write your own context managers when appropriate
data.title: Write your own context managers when appropriate

summaries: Context managers aren't just for files; use them for any setup/teardown pattern.

data.description: Python embraces EAFP (Easier to Ask for Forgiveness than Permission): try the operation and catch exceptions rather than checking preconditions. However, don't use exceptions for normal control flow. Catch specific exceptions (FileNotFoundError FileNotFoundError, ValueError ValueError), not broad Exception Exception. Never use bare except: except: unless you re-raise or have a very good reason. Exceptions should represent actual error conditions.
data.text: Use exceptions for real exceptional cases
data.title: Use exceptions for real exceptional cases

summaries: Exceptions should be specific and intentional, not used for flow control.

data.description: When catching an exception and raising a different one, use raise NewException() from original_exception raise NewException() from original_exception to preserve the stack trace and context. This makes debugging much easier. Use raise raise alone (no arguments) to re-raise the current exception. Never swallow exceptions silently unless you have a documented reason.
data.text: Preserve exception context when re-raising
data.title: Preserve exception context when re-raising

summaries: Use raise from raise from to chain exceptions and preserve context.

data.description: Use try/finally try/finally to ensure cleanup code runs: try: ... finally: cleanup() try: ... finally: cleanup(). Even better, use context managers (with with) which handle this automatically. Never put critical cleanup in bare except blocks—they might not execute if the exception is different than expected. finally finally always runs; else else only runs if no exception occurred.
data.text: Use finally or context managers for cleanup
data.title: Use finally or context managers for cleanup

summaries: Ensure cleanup code runs even if exceptions occur.

data.description: Python supports gradual typing with type hints (PEP 484). Use them for function signatures, especially in public APIs, complex modules, or where types aren't obvious: def greet(name: str) -> str: def greet(name: str) -> str:. Use mypy mypy or similar tools to check types. Don't over-annotate simple code where the intent is already obvious. Type hints are documentation that tools can verify. Modern Python code increasingly uses them.
data.text: Use type hints where they improve clarity
data.title: Use type hints where they improve clarity

summaries: Type hints should make the contract more explicit when they help.

data.description: Optional[T] Optional[T] is shorthand for Union[T, None] Union[T, None]. Use List[int] List[int], Dict[str, int] Dict[str, int] for generic collections (or list[int] list[int], dict[str, int] dict[str, int] in Python 3.9+). Use Protocol Protocol for structural subtyping (duck typing with types). Use TypeVar TypeVar for generic functions. Use Callable[[ArgTypes], ReturnType] Callable[[ArgTypes], ReturnType] for functions. Learn the typing module well if you use type hints extensively.
data.text: Understand common type hint patterns
data.title: Understand common type hint patterns

summaries: Use Optional, Union, List, Dict, Protocol, TypeVar appropriately.

data.description: Deep inheritance hierarchies are hard to understand and maintain. Prefer composition (objects containing other objects) over inheritance. Use mixins sparingly. Use abstract base classes (ABC module) to define interfaces when needed. Python's duck typing often makes formal inheritance unnecessary. Focus on what objects can do, not what they are.
data.text: Prefer composition over inheritance
data.title: Prefer composition over inheritance

summaries: Favor building objects from smaller pieces rather than deep hierarchies.

data.description: Don't write Java-style getters/setters in Python. Use direct attribute access or properties: @property @property decorator for getters, @name.setter @name.setter for setters. This keeps the syntax clean while allowing you to add validation or logic later. Python users expect direct attribute access; properties let you maintain that interface while controlling behavior.
data.text: Use properties for getters and setters
data.title: Use properties for getters and setters

summaries: Properties provide attribute syntax with method behavior.

data.description: Implement __repr__ __repr__ to return a string that could recreate the object: Point(1, 2) Point(1, 2). This is for debugging. Implement __str__ __str__ for user-facing output. If you only implement one, implement __repr__ __repr__. The default __str__ __str__ falls back to __repr__ __repr__. Good __repr__ __repr__ makes debugging much easier. Use f"{obj!r}" f"{obj!r}" to force repr in f-strings.
data.text: Use __str__ __str__ and __repr__ __repr__ appropriately
data.title: Use __str__ __str__ and __repr__ __repr__ appropriately

summaries: __repr__ __repr__ is for developers (unambiguous), __str__ __str__ is for end users (readable).

data.description: Use yield yield to create generator functions that produce values lazily: def fibonacci(): a, b = 0, 1; while True: yield a; a, b = b, a+b def fibonacci(): a, b = 0, 1; while True: yield a; a, b = b, a+b. Generators are memory-efficient for large datasets and infinite sequences. They implement the iterator protocol automatically. Use generator expressions (x for x in items) (x for x in items) for simple cases. Prefer generators over building full lists when processing large data.
data.text: Use generators for lazy sequences
data.title: Use generators for lazy sequences

summaries: Generators produce values on demand, saving memory for large sequences.

data.description: Iterables implement __iter__() __iter__() which returns an iterator. Iterators implement __next__() __next__() which returns the next value or raises StopIteration StopIteration. Generators are the easiest way to create iterators. You can create custom iterators by implementing these methods. Understanding this protocol helps you work with for loops, comprehensions, and iteration tools effectively.
data.text: Understand the iterator protocol
data.title: Understand the iterator protocol

summaries: Iterators implement __iter__ __iter__ and __next__ __next__.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Standard Library and Idioms
data.description: Python's standard library has solutions for most common problems: collections collections (deque, Counter, defaultdict), itertools itertools (efficient iteration tools), functools functools (higher-order functions), pathlib pathlib (path manipulation), dataclasses dataclasses, typing typing, contextlib contextlib, argparse argparse, json json, csv csv, and much more. Learn it well to avoid reinventing wheels and adding unnecessary dependencies.
data.text: Know the standard library well
data.title: Know the standard library well

summaries: Python's standard library is extensive; use it before adding dependencies.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Standard Library and Idioms
data.description: Don't use for i in range(len(items)): item = items[i] for i in range(len(items)): item = items[i]. Use for i, item in enumerate(items): for i, item in enumerate(items): instead. This is more Pythonic, more readable, and less error-prone. If you only need values, use for item in items: for item in items:. If you only need indices (rare), use range.
data.text: Use enumerate enumerate instead of range(len()) range(len())
data.title: Use enumerate enumerate instead of range(len()) range(len())

summaries: enumerate enumerate gives you both index and value in loops.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Standard Library and Idioms
data.description: To iterate over multiple sequences in parallel, use zip zip: for name, score in zip(names, scores): for name, score in zip(names, scores):. zip zip stops when the shortest sequence is exhausted. Use itertools.zip_longest itertools.zip_longest if you need to handle sequences of different lengths. This is more Pythonic than manually indexing multiple lists.
data.text: Use zip zip to iterate over multiple sequences
data.title: Use zip zip to iterate over multiple sequences

summaries: zip zip pairs elements from multiple iterables.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Standard Library and Idioms
data.description: Instead of looping to check conditions, use any() any() and all() all(): if any(user.is_admin for user in users): if any(user.is_admin for user in users): or if all(item.is_valid for item in items): if all(item.is_valid for item in items):. These are more concise and expressive than manual loops. They short-circuit (stop as soon as the result is known), making them efficient.
data.text: Use any any and all all for boolean collections
data.title: Use any any and all all for boolean collections

summaries: any any returns True if any element is truthy; all all if all are.

data.description: Most modern Python projects use pytest. Write test functions starting with test_ test_. Use descriptive names: test_user_creation_with_valid_email test_user_creation_with_valid_email. Use plain assert assert statements (pytest enhances them). Use fixtures for setup. Keep tests focused on one behavior. Tests should be readable and serve as documentation. Parametrize tests with @pytest.mark.parametrize @pytest.mark.parametrize for multiple cases.
data.text: Use pytest-style tests for focused behavior
data.title: Use pytest-style tests for focused behavior

summaries: Python tests should be small, explicit, and easy to read.

data.description: Use unittest.mock unittest.mock or pytest-mock pytest-mock to mock external services, file I/O, network calls. Don't mock the code you're testing—that defeats the purpose. Mocks should simulate external dependencies only. Over-mocking makes tests brittle and coupled to implementation. Prefer real objects when practical. Tests should verify behavior, not implementation.
data.text: Use mocks and patches judiciously
data.title: Use mocks and patches judiciously

summaries: Mock external dependencies, but don't overuse mocks.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Performance and Best Practices
data.description: Use is None is None and is not None is not None for None checks (not == None == None). Use is True is True and is False is False only when you specifically need identity checking (rare). For all other comparisons, use == ==. is is is faster for singletons because it's just pointer comparison. Checking if x is None if x is None is the idiomatic way.
data.text: Use is is for singleton comparisons, == == for value equality
data.title: Use is is for singleton comparisons, == == for value equality

summaries: is is checks object identity; == == checks value equality.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Performance and Best Practices
data.description: Write clear, readable code first. Optimize only when profiling shows a bottleneck. Python has excellent profiling tools (cProfile cProfile, line_profiler line_profiler, memory_profiler memory_profiler). Premature optimization makes code harder to read and maintain. Most Python code is fast enough. When you do optimize, measure before and after to verify improvement. Donald Knuth: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil."
data.text: Don't prematurely optimize; profile first
data.title: Don't prematurely optimize; profile first

summaries: Readable code is more important than premature optimization.

data.category_path: Coding Best Practices/Python/Performance and Best Practices
data.description: Prefer [x*2 for x in items] [x*2 for x in items] over list(map(lambda x: x*2, items)) list(map(lambda x: x*2, items)). Prefer [x for x in items if x > 0] [x for x in items if x > 0] over list(filter(lambda x: x > 0, items)) list(filter(lambda x: x > 0, items)). Comprehensions are clearer, more Pythonic, and don't require lambdas. Use map map/filter filter only when you have an existing named function to pass.
data.text: Use list comprehensions, not map/filter, for simple cases
data.title: Use list comprehensions, not map/filter, for simple cases

summaries: List comprehensions are more Pythonic and readable than map/filter.

data.description: Immutable types can't be changed after creation; methods return new objects. Mutable types can be modified in place. This affects function arguments: mutating a list inside a function affects the caller's list. Understand this to avoid bugs. Tuples are immutable (good for dict keys), lists are not. Strings are immutable; concatenation creates new strings (expensive in loops—use join instead).
data.text: Understand mutable vs immutable types
data.title: Understand mutable vs immutable types

summaries: Strings, tuples, numbers are immutable; lists, dicts, sets are mutable.

data.description: Instead of value = d[key] value = d[key] which raises KeyError KeyError if missing, use value = d.get(key, default_value) value = d.get(key, default_value). Or use defaultdict defaultdict from collections for automatic defaults. Or check with if key in d: if key in d: before accessing. The get get method is concise for simple cases. EAFP style would use try/except KeyError for more complex cases.
data.text: Use dict.get() dict.get() to avoid KeyError
data.title: Use dict.get() dict.get() to avoid KeyError

summaries: dict.get(key, default) dict.get(key, default) safely retrieves values with a fallback.

data.description: Don't use s = s + item s = s + item in a loop; strings are immutable so this creates many temporary objects. Use "".join(items) "".join(items) or collect items in a list and join at the end. For simple concatenation outside loops, + + or f-strings are fine. For building strings in loops, join is the idiomatic and efficient way.
data.text: Use join join for string concatenation in loops
data.title: Use join join for string concatenation in loops

summaries: "".join(items) "".join(items) is much faster than repeated += += for strings.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Layered Architecture
data.description: Layered architecture organizes code into horizontal layers: presentation (UI), application (orchestration), domain (business logic), infrastructure (data access, external services). Each layer should only depend on layers below it, never above. This creates clear separation of concerns and makes testing easier. The domain layer should be independent of infrastructure details. Use dependency inversion (interfaces) to keep domain logic pure. Common in enterprise applications. Avoid the temptation to let infrastructure concerns leak into domain logic.
data.text: Organize code into distinct layers with clear boundaries
data.title: Organize code into distinct layers with clear boundaries

summaries: Separate presentation, business logic, and data access into layers that depend only on layers below them.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Layered Architecture
data.description: The most valuable code in your system is the business logic that embodies your domain understanding. Keep this code free of framework dependencies, database coupling, and infrastructure details. Use ports and adapters (hexagonal architecture) to define interfaces that infrastructure implements. This makes the core logic easier to test, understand, and evolve. Frameworks and databases are details; business logic is the essence. Design so you could swap frameworks or databases without rewriting business rules.
data.text: Keep business logic independent of frameworks and infrastructure
data.title: Keep business logic independent of frameworks and infrastructure

summaries: Core business rules should not depend on databases, web frameworks, or external services.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Microservices Architecture
data.description: Microservices work best when organized around business domains (e.g., Orders, Inventory, Payments) rather than technical concerns (e.g., API Gateway, Database Service). Each service should be independently deployable and own its data—avoid shared databases. Services communicate via well-defined APIs (REST, gRPC, events). This enables teams to work independently and scale services differently. But microservices add complexity: distributed systems are harder to debug, test, and reason about. Start with a modular monolith unless you have clear scaling or organizational needs for microservices.
data.text: Design services around business capabilities, not technical layers
data.title: Design services around business capabilities, not technical layers

summaries: Each microservice should own a complete business capability with its own data store.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Microservices Architecture
data.description: Define explicit contracts between services using API specifications (OpenAPI, gRPC proto files). Version your APIs and maintain backward compatibility when evolving them. Use semantic versioning. Add new fields as optional; deprecate old ones gracefully. Avoid breaking changes; if unavoidable, coordinate carefully. Use consumer-driven contract tests to verify integrations. Clear contracts make services truly independent—teams can evolve their services without breaking others.
data.text: Implement service boundaries with clear contracts
data.title: Implement service boundaries with clear contracts

summaries: Services should communicate through versioned, documented APIs with backward compatibility.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Microservices Architecture
data.description: In distributed systems, failures are normal. Implement timeouts on all remote calls. Use circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures (when a service is down, fail fast rather than overwhelming it). Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter. Use bulkheads to isolate failures. Design for idempotency so retries don't cause duplicate effects. Implement health checks and graceful degradation. Monitor everything. The network is unreliable; your design must account for this.
data.text: Design for failure in distributed systems
data.title: Design for failure in distributed systems

summaries: Microservices must handle network failures, service outages, and partial failures gracefully.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Event-Driven Architecture
data.description: Event-driven architecture decouples services through asynchronous messaging. When something happens (order placed, payment received), publish an event to a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SNS/SQS). Interested services subscribe and react independently. This reduces coupling—publishers don't know about subscribers. Events enable eventual consistency, scalability, and flexibility. But they add complexity: debugging async flows is harder, ensuring message ordering is difficult, and eventual consistency requires careful design. Use events for integration between bounded contexts, not within them.
data.text: Use events for asynchronous communication and decoupling
data.title: Use events for asynchronous communication and decoupling

summaries: Services publish events when state changes; other services subscribe and react independently.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Event-Driven Architecture
data.description: Events represent facts: "OrderPlaced", "PaymentReceived", "UserRegistered". They should be past tense, immutable, and contain all relevant data. Don't design events as commands ("PlaceOrder")—commands are requests that can be rejected; events are facts that happened. Include enough context so consumers don't need to query back. Version events carefully—they're part of your contract. Store events in an event store for audit trails and debugging. Event sourcing takes this further by using events as the primary source of truth.
data.text: Design events as immutable facts about what happened
data.title: Design events as immutable facts about what happened

summaries: Events should describe what occurred, not commands about what to do.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Domain-Driven Design Patterns
data.description: DDD emphasizes close collaboration with domain experts to build a shared understanding. The ubiquitous language is the vocabulary you develop together and use everywhere: in code (class names, method names), in documentation, and in conversations. This reduces translation errors and keeps code aligned with business understanding. If a developer and domain expert can't understand each other's language, the model is wrong. Refactor both code and language together as understanding evolves.
data.text: Model the problem domain with ubiquitous language
data.title: Model the problem domain with ubiquitous language

summaries: Use the same terminology in code, documentation, and conversations with domain experts.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Domain-Driven Design Patterns
data.description: Don't try to create one unified model for the entire system—different parts have different concerns. Bounded contexts are explicit boundaries where a particular model applies. Within a context, maintain a consistent ubiquitous language. Across contexts, use integration patterns (shared kernel, anti-corruption layer, published language). A User in the Ordering context might have different attributes than a User in the Support context—that's okay. Each context can use different technologies and databases. Map contexts explicitly and design their integration points carefully.
data.text: Organize code into bounded contexts with explicit boundaries
data.title: Organize code into bounded contexts with explicit boundaries

summaries: Large systems should be divided into bounded contexts, each with its own model and language.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Software Architecture Patterns/Domain-Driven Design Patterns
data.description: Entities have identity and lifecycle (User, Order). Value objects are immutable and defined by their attributes (Money, Address). Aggregates are consistency boundaries—clusters of entities/value objects with one root entity (Order aggregate might include OrderLines). All external access goes through the aggregate root, which enforces invariants. This prevents invalid states and makes transaction boundaries clear. Keep aggregates small for performance. Domain services handle operations that don't naturally belong to any entity. Repositories provide persistence for aggregate roots. These patterns keep domain logic organized and maintainable.
data.text: Separate domain logic into entities, value objects, and aggregates
data.title: Separate domain logic into entities, value objects, and aggregates

summaries: Use DDD tactical patterns to organize domain logic clearly.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational Patterns
data.description: When object creation is complex or involves choosing between types, use a factory. Factory Method lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related objects. Simple factories (static methods) work for basic cases. Builders handle objects with many optional parameters. Factories improve testability (inject mock factories), hide construction complexity, and make code more flexible. Don't overuse—simple constructors are fine when creation is straightforward.
data.text: Use factory patterns to encapsulate object creation logic
data.title: Use factory patterns to encapsulate object creation logic

summaries: Factories centralize complex construction and enable polymorphic creation.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational Patterns
data.description: Dependency injection inverts control: instead of objects creating their dependencies, they receive them (usually via constructor). This makes dependencies explicit, improves testability (inject mocks), and reduces coupling. DI containers/frameworks automate wiring but aren't required—manual injection (pure DI) is often simpler. Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies, property injection for optional ones. Avoid service locator pattern (asking a global registry for dependencies)—it hides dependencies and makes testing harder.
data.text: Use dependency injection for loose coupling and testability
data.title: Use dependency injection for loose coupling and testability

summaries: Pass dependencies to objects rather than having them create or find dependencies.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural Patterns
data.description: When you need to use an existing class but its interface doesn't match what you need, create an adapter. This is especially useful for integrating third-party libraries or legacy code. The adapter implements the interface you need and delegates to the adaptee. Anti-corruption layers in DDD are essentially adapters that protect your domain from external models. Adapters enable you to change external dependencies without affecting core code.
data.text: Use adapter pattern to integrate incompatible interfaces
data.title: Use adapter pattern to integrate incompatible interfaces

summaries: Adapters translate between interfaces without modifying existing code.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural Patterns
data.description: Decorators add behavior to objects dynamically without subclassing. They implement the same interface as the object they wrap. Common uses: logging, caching, transaction management, authentication. In languages with function decorators (Python, TypeScript), use those. Otherwise, use explicit decorator classes. This follows Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification. Decorators can be composed (stack multiple decorators). Middleware in web frameworks are decorators.
data.text: Use decorator pattern to add behavior without modifying classes
data.title: Use decorator pattern to add behavior without modifying classes

summaries: Decorators wrap objects to extend functionality, following Open/Closed Principle.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural Patterns
data.description: Repositories encapsulate data access logic and provide a domain-oriented API: userRepository.findByEmail(email) userRepository.findByEmail(email) not db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE...") db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE..."). This keeps SQL/database concerns out of business logic. Repositories return domain objects, not DTOs or database records. Each aggregate root gets a repository. This improves testability (mock repositories) and makes it easier to change data stores. Avoid generic repositories that expose too much—design repositories around domain needs, not CRUD operations.
sources: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Martin Fowler)
data.text: Use repository pattern to abstract data access
data.title: Use repository pattern to abstract data access

summaries: Repositories provide a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral Patterns
data.description: Strategy pattern encapsulates algorithms behind an interface, allowing them to vary independently. Use it for: payment methods, sorting algorithms, validation rules, pricing strategies. The context uses a strategy interface; concrete strategies implement the algorithm. This eliminates conditionals, makes adding new strategies easy, and improves testability. In functional languages, strategies can be functions. Common in Go (interfaces with single methods), Java (functional interfaces), and modern languages with first-class functions.
data.text: Use strategy pattern to make algorithms interchangeable
data.title: Use strategy pattern to make algorithms interchangeable

summaries: Define a family of algorithms and make them interchangeable through a common interface.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral Patterns
data.description: Observer pattern implements publish-subscribe: subjects notify observers when state changes. Observers register with subjects, get notified, and react independently. This decouples components—subjects don't know about specific observers. Common uses: UI updates (MVC, reactive frameworks), event handling, logging. Modern implementations use event emitters, reactive streams (RxJS, Reactor), or message brokers. Be cautious of memory leaks (observers not unregistering) and circular notifications.
data.text: Use observer pattern for decoupled event handling
data.title: Use observer pattern for decoupled event handling

summaries: Observers subscribe to subjects and get notified of state changes.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/RESTful API Design
data.description: REST APIs model resources as nouns: /users /users, /orders /orders, /products/{id} /products/{id}. Use HTTP methods for actions: GET (retrieve), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove). URLs should be plural nouns. Avoid verbs in URLs (/getUser /getUser is wrong). Use nested resources for relationships: /orders/{id}/items /orders/{id}/items. Return appropriate status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error. Design for resources, not RPC-style operations.
data.text: Design REST APIs around resources, not actions
data.title: Design REST APIs around resources, not actions

summaries: URLs should represent resources; HTTP methods represent actions.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/RESTful API Design
data.description: Use correct status codes: 2xx for success, 3xx for redirection, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors. Be specific: 400 (bad request), 401 (unauthenticated), 403 (forbidden), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict), 422 (validation error), 429 (rate limited). Return structured error responses with error codes, messages, and field-level validation errors. Don't return 200 with {success: false} {success: false} in the body—use proper status codes. Consistent error handling makes APIs easier to use.
data.text: Use proper HTTP status codes and error responses
data.title: Use proper HTTP status codes and error responses

summaries: Status codes communicate results; error responses provide actionable details.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/RESTful API Design
data.description: Version APIs through URL (/v1/users /v1/users), headers (Accept: application/vnd.api+json; version=1 Accept: application/vnd.api+json; version=1), or query parameters. URL versioning is most visible. Introduce breaking changes in new versions only. Within a version, maintain backward compatibility: add optional fields, don't remove or rename fields, don't change semantics. Deprecate old versions gracefully with clear timelines. Document migration paths. Semantic versioning helps: major version for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. Consider API gateways for versioning logic.
data.text: Version APIs explicitly and maintain backward compatibility
data.title: Version APIs explicitly and maintain backward compatibility

summaries: APIs must evolve without breaking existing clients.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/RESTful API Design
data.description: For collection endpoints, support: pagination (offset/limit or cursor-based), filtering (?status=active ?status=active), sorting (?sort=-createdAt ?sort=-createdAt), field selection (?fields=id,name ?fields=id,name). Return pagination metadata: total count, next/previous links. Use cursor-based pagination for large datasets. Be consistent across all endpoints. Document query parameters. Consider GraphQL if clients need flexible querying. Rate limiting and caching headers are important for large collections.
data.text: Implement pagination, filtering, and sorting consistently
data.title: Implement pagination, filtering, and sorting consistently

summaries: Collections should support pagination, filtering, sorting, and field selection.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/gRPC and RPC API Design
data.description: Design gRPC services with clear method names and message types. Use Proto3 for modern APIs. Add field numbers carefully—they're part of your contract. Use reserved keywords for removed fields. Add optional/required appropriately. Group related RPCs in services. Use streaming RPCs for large data or real-time updates. Document services and messages thoroughly—proto comments become API docs. Consider backward compatibility: add new fields, don't remove or change types of existing ones. Use semantic versioning for proto packages.
data.text: Define clear, versioned service contracts with Protocol Buffers
data.title: Define clear, versioned service contracts with Protocol Buffers

summaries: gRPC services should have well-documented proto definitions with evolution in mind.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/gRPC and RPC API Design
data.description: Unary RPCs (request-response) for simple operations. Server streaming for returning large result sets (pagination, log streaming). Client streaming for uploading data. Bidirectional streaming for real-time communication (chat, multiplayer games). Streaming improves performance for large data and enables low-latency communication. But streaming is more complex—handle errors, backpressure, cancellation carefully. Don't use streaming if request-response suffices. gRPC's performance benefits apply to all types.
data.text: Choose appropriate RPC types for your use case
data.title: Choose appropriate RPC types for your use case

summaries: Unary, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming serve different needs.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/GraphQL API Design
data.description: GraphQL schemas should reflect how clients want to consume data, not your database structure. Use types for entities, fields for attributes and relationships. Queries for reads, mutations for writes, subscriptions for real-time updates. Design resolvers to fetch data efficiently—avoid N+1 queries with DataLoader. Use nullable vs non-nullable carefully. Deprecate fields instead of removing them. GraphQL works best when it provides a unified API across multiple services. But it shifts complexity to the server—caching and query optimization are harder than with REST.
data.text: Design GraphQL schemas around the client's data needs
data.title: Design GraphQL schemas around the client's data needs

summaries: GraphQL lets clients specify exactly what data they need; design the schema accordingly.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/API Design Principles/GraphQL API Design
data.description: GraphQL clients can request arbitrary data and deeply nested queries. Implement field-level authorization—just because a user can query a User doesn't mean they can see all fields. Use query complexity analysis to prevent expensive queries. Implement depth limits, rate limiting, and timeouts. Consider persisted queries (pre-approved query whitelist) for production. Monitor query patterns to identify performance issues. GraphQL's power requires robust safeguards.
data.text: Implement proper authorization and query complexity limits
data.title: Implement proper authorization and query complexity limits

summaries: GraphQL's flexibility requires careful security and performance controls.

data.category: What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.description: Verify the code solves the stated problem correctly. Check error handling: are errors caught, logged, and handled appropriately? Look for edge cases: empty inputs, null values, boundary conditions, concurrent access. Check assumptions—are they documented and validated? Look for off-by-one errors, incorrect comparisons, timezone issues, encoding problems. Test coverage should include happy path and error cases. Correctness is the most important review criterion.
data.text: Check for correctness and edge case handling
data.title: Check for correctness and edge case handling

summaries: Does the code do what it's supposed to do, including error and boundary cases?

data.category: What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.description: Code should be self-explanatory through good naming, clear structure, and appropriate comments. Check: Are names descriptive? Is the structure logical? Are functions small and focused? Is complexity justified? Are comments explaining why, not what? Is the code consistent with the project's style? Readability matters more than cleverness. Code is read 10x more than it's written—optimize for readers. If you have to ask "what does this do?", it needs improvement.
data.text: Evaluate code readability and maintainability
data.title: Evaluate code readability and maintainability

summaries: Can other developers understand and modify this code easily?

data.category: What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.description: Check that code fits the existing architecture. Look for: proper layer separation, appropriate use of interfaces, correct dependency direction (high-level doesn't depend on low-level), reasonable abstractions, and adherence to SOLID principles. Watch for God objects, tight coupling, hidden dependencies, and violations of single responsibility. New code should improve the codebase, not add technical debt. If the design is questionable, discuss before implementation is complete.
data.text: Verify architectural consistency and design quality
data.title: Verify architectural consistency and design quality

summaries: Does the code follow established patterns and maintain good boundaries?

data.category: What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.description: Look for N+1 queries, unnecessary loops, inefficient algorithms, excessive allocations, resource leaks (unclosed files/connections), missing indexes. Check that expensive operations are cached or optimized. Look for blocking operations on critical paths. However, don't prematurely optimize—focus on obvious problems. Profile before optimizing non-obvious cases. Consider whether the code will scale with realistic data volumes. Performance issues are easier to fix early.
data.text: Assess performance and resource usage
data.title: Assess performance and resource usage

summaries: Are there obvious performance issues or resource leaks?

data.category: What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.description: Review tests alongside code. Check: Are tests clear and focused? Do they test behavior, not implementation? Is coverage adequate (especially for edge cases and error paths)? Are tests deterministic and independent? Is the code designed for testability (dependency injection, small functions, clear interfaces)? Integration tests for workflows, unit tests for logic. Tests are documentation—they show how code should be used. Missing or poor tests are a red flag.
data.text: Ensure proper testing and testability
data.title: Ensure proper testing and testability

summaries: Is the code testable and adequately tested?

data.category: What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/What to Look for in Code Reviews
data.description: Look for: SQL injection (use parameterized queries), XSS (escape output), authentication/authorization issues, exposed secrets (API keys in code), insecure defaults, unvalidated input, information leaks in errors, missing encryption for sensitive data. Check compliance with data protection regulations (GDPR, CCPA). Verify that user input is validated, sanitized, and handled safely. Security bugs are expensive; catch them in review.
data.text: Check security and data handling practices
data.title: Check security and data handling practices

summaries: Are there security vulnerabilities or data protection issues?

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/Code Review Process Best Practices
data.description: Aim for PRs under 400 lines of code. Large PRs are hard to review well—reviewers get fatigued and miss issues. Break work into logical chunks. Each PR should have a single, clear purpose. Small PRs enable faster feedback cycles and easier rollbacks if issues arise. If a change must be large, consider breaking it into a series of PRs or providing extra context (design doc, video walkthrough).
data.text: Keep changes small and focused
data.title: Keep changes small and focused

summaries: Smaller pull requests are reviewed more thoroughly and merged faster.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/Code Review Process Best Practices
