data.description: Good PR descriptions include: what problem you're solving, how you solved it, what alternatives you considered, how to test/verify the change, any potential risks. Link to relevant tickets/docs. Screenshots/videos for UI changes. Call out areas where you want specific feedback. This context helps reviewers understand your choices and review more effectively. Don't assume reviewers know the background.
data.text: Write clear PR descriptions with context
data.title: Write clear PR descriptions with context

summaries: Explain what changed, why, and how to test it.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Code Review Best Practices/Code Review Process Best Practices
data.description: Good review comments: point to specific lines, explain the issue, suggest alternatives, cite standards/docs when applicable. Use "we" not "you" ("we should handle nulls here"). Distinguish between must-fix issues and suggestions. Praise good solutions. Avoid "just" and "simply"—they're condescending. Ask questions instead of making demands. Remember: you're reviewing code, not judging the author. The goal is to improve the code and share knowledge, not to show off or criticize.
sources: How to Do Code Reviews Like a Human (Michael Lynch)
data.text: Give actionable, respectful feedback
data.title: Give actionable, respectful feedback

summaries: Comments should be specific, constructive, and focus on the code, not the person.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Testing Strategies/Test Pyramid
data.description: The test pyramid: broad base of fast, focused unit tests; middle layer of integration tests verifying components work together; small top layer of expensive, slow end-to-end tests. Unit tests are cheap, fast, and easy to maintain—use them extensively for business logic. Integration tests verify interactions (database, external services)—slower but necessary. E2E tests verify full user workflows—expensive and brittle, use sparingly for critical paths only. Inverted pyramids (mostly E2E tests) are slow and fragile.
data.text: Structure tests as a pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few E2E tests
data.title: Structure tests as a pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few E2E tests

summaries: Different test types have different costs and benefits; balance them appropriately.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Testing Strategies/Unit Testing Principles
data.description: Tests should interact with code through its public API and verify observable behavior. Don't test private methods directly—test them through public methods. Don't assert on internal state unless necessary. This makes tests resilient to refactoring. If you refactor and all tests break, they're too coupled to implementation. Good tests: arrange inputs, call public methods, assert observable outputs/side effects. Think like a user of the API, not its implementer.
data.text: Test behavior, not implementation details
data.title: Test behavior, not implementation details

summaries: Tests should verify what code does, not how it does it.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Testing Strategies/Unit Testing Principles
data.description: Unit tests should be FIRST: Fast (milliseconds), Independent (no shared state), Repeatable (deterministic), Self-validating (pass/fail, no manual inspection), Timely (written with or before code). One logical assertion per test. Use descriptive names that explain what's being tested. Avoid test interdependencies—tests should pass in any order. Use test fixtures/setup for common initialization, but be careful not to hide important context. Fast, focused tests give rapid feedback and encourage running tests frequently.
data.text: Keep tests focused, fast, and independent
data.title: Keep tests focused, fast, and independent

summaries: Each test should verify one thing and run quickly without depending on other tests.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Testing Strategies/Integration Testing
data.description: Integration tests verify that your code works with real external systems. Test database operations with a real database (use test containers or in-memory databases). Test API integrations with real endpoints (use test instances or contract tests). Test message handling with real brokers. These tests are slower than unit tests but catch issues unit tests can't. Use them judiciously—not every path needs integration tests, just critical interactions. Consider contract testing (Pact) for API integrations.
data.text: Use integration tests to verify component interactions
data.title: Use integration tests to verify component interactions

summaries: Test that components work together correctly: database, external APIs, message queues.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Testing Strategies/End-to-End Testing
data.description: E2E tests verify complete user workflows through the entire system. They're slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain. Use them for: critical business flows (signup, checkout, payment), smoke tests (is the system alive?), and workflows that cross many components. Don't use E2E tests to verify edge cases—that's what unit tests are for. Keep E2E tests stable by using good selectors, explicit waits, and retry logic. Run them less frequently (nightly builds, pre-release). Consider API-level E2E tests instead of UI tests when possible.
sources: Testing Strategies in a Microservice Architecture (Toby Clemson)
data.text: Reserve E2E tests for critical user journeys
data.title: Reserve E2E tests for critical user journeys

summaries: E2E tests are expensive; use them for high-value, business-critical workflows only.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Testing Strategies/Test Doubles and Mocking
data.description: Test doubles replace dependencies: stubs return predetermined values, mocks verify interactions, fakes are working implementations (in-memory database). Use them to isolate the unit under test and control test conditions. But over-mocking makes tests brittle and couples them to implementation. Prefer real objects when practical. Mock I/O boundaries (HTTP, database, file system), not domain objects. Be especially careful with partial mocks—they're usually a design smell. If mocking is painful, the design might need improvement.
data.text: Use test doubles strategically to isolate units under test
data.title: Use test doubles strategically to isolate units under test

summaries: Mocks, stubs, and fakes enable focused testing but can make tests brittle.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Security Best Practices/Input Validation and Sanitization
data.description: All input from users, APIs, file uploads, or external systems is untrusted. Validate early: check types, lengths, formats, ranges. Use allowlists (known good values) not denylists (known bad values). Sanitize input before use: escape for context (HTML, SQL, shell), strip dangerous characters. Reject invalid input with clear error messages. This prevents injection attacks (SQL, XSS, command injection), buffer overflows, and malformed data issues. Input validation is your first line of defense.
data.text: Validate and sanitize all external input
data.title: Validate and sanitize all external input

summaries: Never trust user input; validate, sanitize, and enforce constraints.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Security Best Practices/Input Validation and Sanitization
data.description: SQL injection is still a top vulnerability. Always use parameterized queries/prepared statements: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ? SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ? with parameter binding, never SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}' SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'. ORMs usually handle this correctly, but verify. Even "safe" input can be dangerous. Parameterized queries prevent injection by keeping data separate from code. This applies to all databases. No exceptions.
sources: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
data.text: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection
data.title: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection

summaries: Never concatenate user input into SQL queries; use parameters instead.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Security Best Practices/Authentication and Authorization
data.description: Strong authentication requires: password requirements (length, complexity, no common passwords), secure hashing (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt—never MD5/SHA1), MFA for sensitive operations, rate limiting on login attempts, account lockout for brute force protection, secure session management (HTTPOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies), password reset flows that don't leak information. Use established authentication libraries/services (Auth0, OAuth2) rather than rolling your own. Authentication bugs are expensive.
data.text: Implement defense in depth for authentication
data.title: Implement defense in depth for authentication

summaries: Use multiple security layers: strong passwords, MFA, rate limiting, session management.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Security Best Practices/Authentication and Authorization
data.description: Authorization must be enforced consistently: check permissions on every API endpoint, every database query, every business operation. Don't rely on UI hiding for security—users can bypass UIs. Check authorization after authentication. Use role-based or attribute-based access control. Default to deny—require explicit grants. Be especially careful with horizontal authorization (user A accessing user B's data). Log authorization failures. Test authorization thoroughly including edge cases. Many breaches result from authorization bugs.
data.text: Implement proper authorization checks at every layer
data.title: Implement proper authorization checks at every layer

summaries: Verify permissions on every operation, not just at entry points.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Security Best Practices/Secrets Management
data.description: Never hardcode secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens, certificates) in code or commit them to git. Use environment variables, secret management services (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault), or configuration files excluded from version control. Rotate secrets regularly. Use different secrets for different environments. Scan repositories for accidentally committed secrets (git-secrets, truffleHog). If a secret is committed, assume it's compromised—rotate immediately and investigate. Git history persists forever.
data.text: Never commit secrets to version control
data.title: Never commit secrets to version control

summaries: Use environment variables, secret managers, or vaults for sensitive data.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Security Best Practices/Secure Communication
data.description: Use HTTPS (TLS 1.2+) for all web traffic. Use TLS for database connections, internal service communication, and API calls. Don't allow fallback to unencrypted connections. Validate certificates properly—don't disable verification in production. Use HSTS headers to enforce HTTPS. Encrypt sensitive data at rest as well. Consider mutual TLS for service-to-service authentication. Network traffic can be intercepted; encryption is essential.
sources: OWASP Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet
data.text: Use TLS for all network communication
data.title: Use TLS for all network communication

summaries: Encrypt data in transit; don't send sensitive data over unencrypted connections.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Performance Optimization Patterns/Database Performance
data.description: Analyze query patterns and add indexes on: WHERE clause columns, JOIN columns, ORDER BY columns, frequently queried foreign keys. Composite indexes for multi-column queries (order matters: most selective first). Don't over-index—each index costs write performance and storage. Use EXPLAIN/ANALYZE to verify indexes are used. Consider covering indexes (include all columns needed by a query). Monitor slow queries and add indexes iteratively. Different databases have different index types (B-tree, hash, GiN, GiST)—choose appropriately.
data.text: Design indexes to match query patterns
data.title: Design indexes to match query patterns

summaries: Indexes speed up queries but slow down writes; design them strategically.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Performance Optimization Patterns/Database Performance
data.description: N+1 queries occur when you load a collection and then query for each item's relationships: one query for the list, N queries for related data. This is catastrophic for performance. Solutions: eager loading (JOIN or separate batch query), lazy loading with batching (DataLoader in GraphQL), caching. ORMs make N+1 easy to accidentally create—use query analyzers to detect. Profile database queries in development. One query returning 1000 rows is much faster than 1000 queries returning one row each.
data.text: Avoid N+1 query problems
data.title: Avoid N+1 query problems

summaries: Load related data eagerly or batch queries to prevent excessive database roundtrips.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Performance Optimization Patterns/Caching Strategies
data.description: Caching improves performance dramatically but adds complexity. Cache at multiple levels: CDN (static assets), HTTP cache (response caching with ETags/Cache-Control), application cache (Redis, Memcached), database query cache. Choose TTL-based expiration for data that can be stale, or implement cache invalidation for data that must be fresh. Consider read-through, write-through, write-behind patterns. Remember: cache invalidation is hard—Phil Karlton said there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.
data.text: Implement caching at multiple layers
data.title: Implement caching at multiple layers

summaries: Cache aggressively but invalidate correctly; use appropriate cache levels.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Performance Optimization Patterns/Caching Strategies
data.description: Cache-aside: application checks cache, queries on miss, updates cache. Read-through: cache loads data on miss. Write-through: writes go through cache to database. Write-behind: cache buffers writes. Refresh-ahead: proactively refresh before expiration. Choose based on: read/write ratio, consistency requirements, failure modes. Cache-aside is most common and flexible. Consider cache warming for critical data. Monitor hit rates. Distributed caches need thoughtful key design and eviction policies.
data.text: Use the right caching pattern for your needs
data.title: Use the right caching pattern for your needs

summaries: Different caching patterns suit different requirements.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Performance Optimization Patterns/Asynchronous Processing
data.description: Long-running operations (sending emails, generating reports, image processing, external API calls) should be asynchronous. Return immediately to the user and process in the background. Use job queues (Sidekiq, Celery, Bull, AWS SQS) with workers. Make jobs idempotent (safe to retry). Implement retry with exponential backoff. Provide status updates (webhooks, polling, WebSockets). This improves user experience and system resilience. But async adds complexity: debugging is harder, monitoring is essential, eventual consistency requires careful design.
data.text: Offload slow operations to background jobs
data.title: Offload slow operations to background jobs

summaries: Don't make users wait for slow operations; process them asynchronously.

data.category_path: Architecture and Design Patterns/Performance Optimization Patterns/Resource Management
data.description: Opening database connections, HTTP connections, or other network connections is expensive. Use connection pools to reuse connections. Configure pool size appropriately: too small causes queuing, too large exhausts server resources. Monitor pool usage—exhausted pools indicate performance issues. Most frameworks provide pooling (database drivers, HTTP clients). For serverless, consider connection management strategies (connection poolers like PgBouncer, HTTP keep-alive). Proper connection management prevents resource exhaustion.
data.text: Use connection pooling for database and external service connections
data.title: Use connection pooling for database and external service connections

summaries: Creating connections is expensive; reuse them through pooling.

They apply proven patterns from your knowledge base, catch common mistakes before you see them, suggest the right approach for each task, and learn from your feedback to get better over time. AI analyzes your request and picks relevant Spaces automatically. For example, "implement user authentication" uses go-best-practices and security-guidelines, while "fix this test failure" uses testing-patterns and debugging-checklist. Generated code is automatically checked against Space rules. If validation finds issues, AI fixes them (up to 2 attempts) so you get corrected code on the first try.

data.description: Commands can run in two modes. Terminal Mode opens OS native terminal window where interactive prompts work (passwords, confirmations), terminal stays open after completion, best for: sudo sudo, ssh ssh, vim vim, top top, tail -f tail -f. Background Mode runs invisibly, captures output, results shown in chat, no interaction possible, best for: ls ls, pwd pwd, git status git status, cat file.txt cat file.txt. Smart defaults automatically suggest the right mode. Terminal for: sudo sudo, ssh ssh, editors, monitors. Background for: directory ops, file viewing, git queries. You can always override the suggestion. Example sudo command (auto-terminal): User asks "Run sudo apt update", approval modal suggests terminal mode, user clicks Allow, command launches in terminal window for password input. Example simple command (auto-background): User asks "Show current directory", approval modal defaults to background, user clicks Allow, local command executed with output shown directly.

Action types: Shell Commands (local_shell_execution local_shell_execution) and Code Patches (coding_workflow_patch coding_workflow_patch). data.description: After Spaces are used, you'll see feedback buttons: "👍 Helpful" and "👎 Needs Work". Click Helpful when: code works correctly on first try, patterns match your team's style, error handling is appropriate, tests are well-structured. Click Needs Work when: code doesn't match requirements, patterns feel too strict or loose, better approach should have been used, validation missed real issues. Why feedback matters: good feedback means Space used more often for similar tasks, negative feedback means Space used less and alternatives tried, system learns your preferences over time. Privacy: feedback stored locally, no code sent to external servers.

data.description: Stores vs Spaces: Stores handle structured data persistence (databases, transactions, CRUD operations). Spaces handle semantic memory (knowledge, categories, retrieval). Both coexist but serve different purposes. This separation keeps deterministic persistence and semantic retrieval aligned without forcing them into one abstraction.
